data.Description: Top-level mental model and router. Defines what an Effortless project is, the load-bearing axioms, the schema-change decision tree, the Token Discipline rule, the no-migrations guardrail, and the routing table to every other skill.
data.WhyItExists: Without a top-level frame, Claude improvises — and improvisation in ERB means editing generated SQL and reimplementing business logic in app code. The orchestrator keeps the model coherent across whatever sub-skill is loaded next.

data.Description: Turns any folder into an Effortless project: runs effortless -init, creates the standard layout, writes the project CLAUDE.md, and generates start.sh.
data.WhyItExists: Without the CLAUDE.md marker, future Claude sessions can't recognize the project as Effortless and the rest of the suite won't load. This skill installs the gate that opens everything else.

data.Description: The Shadle steps: raw text to vocabulary to glossary to narrative to mock data to schema to a populated effortless-rulebook.json (rulebook-first; Airtable/Excel mirror is optional and downstream).
data.WhyItExists: Going from 'here's what we want to build' to 'we have a formal rulebook' is the fuzziest part of ERB. This skill is the structured pipeline for that translation, so you don't end up with a half-formal mess that can't be projected to a substrate.

data.Description: First-run setup for Postgres-targeted projects: preflight tool checks, install transpilers, get a rulebook in place (authored directly, or seeded from an optional Airtable/Excel surface), generate SQL, init the local DB. Sets up the regenerate-from-scratch shape (init-db.sh drops + recreates), not an incremental-migrations shape.
data.WhyItExists: Gets you from 'I have a rulebook (or an upstream surface to seed it)' to 'I have a working local DB + generated views' without remembering the per-step cd discipline that makes the build work. This is the only step where commits without asking are appropriate (it's a known-good bootstrap sequence).

data.Description: The iterative ERB development cycle: CHANGE-RULE in the rulebook (directly, or via a connected input spoke), then effortless build, then CONSUME generated views in app code, repeat. Includes the migration anti-pattern (the #1 way the loop gets bypassed).
data.WhyItExists: Without it you regress to 'naked Claude' — hand-maintaining schema in three places (DB migration, ORM model, API serializer) and breaking sync every time something changes. The loop is what makes ERB feel effortless instead of redundant.

data.Description: Everything about the skill set itself: check whether your local clone is behind upstream, apply updates, add/edit/deprecate skills.
data.WhyItExists: The skill set is its own moving target — new skills get added, old ones get merged, conventions drift. This skill is the maintenance interface for the suite (separate from the CLI binary, which is effortless-cli).

data.Description: Both installing/updating the effortless binary and using its commands. Covers prerequisites, install paths, login flow, -init, -setAccountAPIKey, transpiler installation, build flags.
data.WhyItExists: Nothing in the rest of the suite works without the CLI being on PATH and pointing at the right Node version. This skill is also where the 'effortless: command not found' recovery flow lives.

data.Description: Install and use the always-on Effortless MCP server — the streamable-HTTP endpoint that exposes ~54 transpiler tools plus the effortless-claude skill set as MCP Resources to any MCP-compatible agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, ChatGPT, etc.).
data.WhyItExists: The CLI binary is not the only way to drive the catalog — MCP is the protocol-level surface that lets non-Claude agents (and Claude in non-CLI contexts) call transpilers, run builds, query rulebooks, and read skills without anything installed locally. Without this skill, Claude improvises wiring instructions and tells users to paste handcrafted JSON into the wrong config file.

data.Description: Naming rules (Name is a calculated display alias, never the stored PK/match key; PascalCase plural tables; singular FKs with no Id suffix; plural reverse FKs); DAG structure (1-to-many only, no cycles, no many-to-many); surrogate-key policy.
data.WhyItExists: These rules look arbitrary until you realize they're what makes the substrate-equivalence guarantee hold. Read this before 'fixing' something the linter complains about, because the linter is usually right.

data.Description: Reference for the structure of effortless-rulebook.json: top-level keys, table objects, field schema, the five field types, datatypes, formula syntax, the _meta section.
data.WhyItExists: When you need to know 'what does a calculated field look like in JSON' or 'how is a relationship encoded', you want a 1-screen reference, not to grep through example rulebooks.

data.Description: Targeted, token-efficient one-liners against effortless-rulebook.json: list tables, extract schema for one table, find FK relationships, inspect calculated fields and formulas.
data.WhyItExists: The rulebook can be megabytes once it has data. Reading it whole burns your context window for nothing — you only ever needed the schema fragment for one table. This skill keeps you in the lightweight-query habit.

data.Description: The input-spoke options for making changes, all writing to the same rulebook hub: rulebook-direct (best practice), an optional upstream grid (Airtable/Excel), and reverse-sync via build -id. Permission checkpoints. Carries the canonical NO-MIGRATIONS rule for local-dev (regenerate from scratch via init-db.sh; never write SQL migrations).
data.WhyItExists: Most 'this didn't work' stories in ERB are someone editing a generated output (SQL, app code) instead of the rulebook hub, then effortless build overwriting their edits. This skill is the discipline that keeps every change landing on the hub.

data.Description: How effortless.json, ProjectTranspilers, and effortless build actually work: the catalog of transpilers, the -id flag, multi-substrate architecture, and the two deployment shapes (local-dev = regenerate via init-db.sh; bases = migrations via apply-migration.sh).
data.WhyItExists: When the build does something surprising — a transpiler doesn't run, a generated file lands in the wrong directory, -id does something different than build — this skill is the 'how does the pipeline actually work' reference.

data.Description: Canonical home for the Airtable-API mechanics, used only when the project opted into Airtable as an input spoke (one optional editing surface, sibling to Excel/Notion): scalar field add/modify/rename, table creation (without formulas), and all CRUD via the REST API. Other skills point here rather than repeating the key-resolution and -account airtable details.
data.WhyItExists: When a project does use Airtable, about 80% of changes are scalar fields or CRUD — the API handles them in a few seconds, and falling back to OMNI (Playwright) for these is wasteful. Keeping the mechanics in one place lets the rest of the suite stay rulebook-first and just reference this skill.

data.Description: The escape hatch for what the API can't do: formula fields, lookup fields, rollup fields, and new-table creation. Includes the bundled Playwright script that drives a headed Chrome to OMNI.
data.WhyItExists: Without this skill Claude either can't add a formula field at all, or wastes everyone's time generating OMNI prompts for you to copy-paste manually. With it, formula/lookup/rollup work happens automatically.

data.Description: Patterns for the generated SQL: read from vw_* views (never base tables), never edit 00–05 files, customize via *b-customize-*.sql and the ERBCustomizations table only when the rulebook can't express the rule. Local-dev has no migrations folder — init-db.sh regenerates from scratch.
data.WhyItExists: This is where most 'fixes' go wrong: someone edits 02-create-functions.sql to 'patch' a behavior, the next build erases it, the bug comes back, and now there's a phantom commit history with no surviving code. This skill prevents that whole class of incident.

data.Description: End-to-end 'create a base + magic-links tenant + RLS-secured app in 5 minutes' flow on bases.effortlessapi.com. The lone ERB deployment shape that uses migrations (via postgres/apply-migration.sh) because bases-hosted DBs can't be dropped.
data.WhyItExists: When you want a hosted Postgres + auth without setting up a backend, this is the shortest path from zero to 'users can log in and only see their own data'. The skill encodes the gotchas that aren't in the docs.

data.Description: Add passwordless email-code (magic-link) auth to any Postgres-backed app, not just bases.effortlessapi.com. Mints a tenant on magiclink.effortlessapi.com, wires Authorization: Bearer middleware, optionally installs app.jwt_*() SQL helpers for RLS.
data.WhyItExists: Magic-links is a notary, not a referee — it just verifies 'we sent code C to email E, the holder returned it.' That clean separation means you can layer it onto any existing app without rewriting your user model. This skill encodes the wiring.

data.Description: DAG validation (find missing FK targets), broken-FK checks, JOIN anti-pattern detection in app code, legacy-code migration helpers (rewrite base-table reads to view reads).
data.WhyItExists: ERB projects accumulate two kinds of debt: rulebook entries with broken references (deleted tables, renamed FKs), and app code that reads from base tables instead of views. Both compound silently. This skill surfaces them.

data.Description: The conceptual floor: SDLAF, the bitemporal ACID DAG, the 5 primitives, what the Conceptual Model Completeness Conjecture predicts and forbids.
data.WhyItExists: When someone asks 'WHY is ERB structured this way? Isn't this overkill?' — improvising the answer makes it sound arbitrary. This skill grounds the answer in the conjecture, so the response is consistent across sessions.

data.Description: The empirical demonstration: 11+ substrates (including ARM64, COBOL, OWL/SHACL, English), the conformance suite, ExplainDAG, answer-key.json. Pointer into github.com/effortlessapi/effortless-rulebooks.
data.WhyItExists: When the response to 'does this actually work?' needs to be 'yes, here's the runnable proof' — this skill is the catalog of runnable proofs.

data.Description: Skeptic-facing answers, strictly grounded in receipts (papers, repos, runnable demos). Common objections paired with cited responses.
data.WhyItExists: When the methodology needs to be defended (to a skeptical reviewer, an architecture committee, a Hacker News thread), the responses should cite, not enthuse. This skill enforces that.

data.Description: The OSS catalog: every public repo in the SSoTme and effortlessapi GitHub orgs, with one-liner descriptions and install snippets.
data.WhyItExists: 'Where is the source for X?' / 'Is there a transpiler for Y?' come up constantly. Without this skill, Claude guesses; with it, the answer is cited.

data.Description: Add Excel export to any Effortless Postgres project: populate a rulebook-export.json from live vw_* views, run rulebook-to-xlsx, and wire a download endpoint + link into the app.
data.WhyItExists: Any ERB project can export its full current state — schema + live data + all calculated fields — as a multi-sheet Excel workbook. This skill makes it a single turn of the loop to add that capability.

data.Description: Spin up a complete Effortless POC demo app from a one- or two-sentence domain description — no Airtable, no Shadle steps. Fastest path from 'make this an effortless demo for X' to a running Express + Vite SPA backed by a Postgres-generated rulebook with a multi-hop calculated-field DAG the UI exercises end-to-end.
data.WhyItExists: Without this skill, 'make me a quick demo' either drags in the full Airtable/bootstrap pipeline or gets hand-coded outside the rulebook entirely. This skill is the direct, no-detour path from a one-liner to a running, rulebook-first proof.

data.Description: Generate plain-English RuleSpeak documentation from an effortless-rulebook.json — declarative business rules, vocabulary, fact types, definitional rules (DR-n), traceability back to formulas. Installs rulebook-to-rulespeak and emits rulespeak/rulespeak.md + .html on every build.
data.WhyItExists: A rulebook is only as useful as a non-technical stakeholder's ability to read it. Without this skill, a newly-authored rulebook has no plain-English artifact and reviewers are stuck reading JSON. Default install whenever a rulebook is created.

data.Description: Set up an Effortless project with SQL Server as the execution substrate — install rulebook-to-sql-server, generate T-SQL under sql-server/, run init-db.sh via sqlcmd, wire an Express app to mssql. Mirrors effortless-setup-postgres for the SQL Server path.
data.WhyItExists: Not every substrate is Postgres. Without this skill, a SQL-Server-targeted project either gets force-fit into the Postgres skill's assumptions or hand-built outside the rulebook pipeline entirely.

data.Description: The canonical reference for the exact effortless.json schema — ProjectTranspilers entries, the ssotme:// protocol, correct CLI flag shapes. Load before emitting any effortless.json content, even a partial snippet.
data.WhyItExists: effortless.json is hand-authored exactly once per project and then owned by the CLI. Without this skill, Claude hallucinates key names (Transpilers vs ProjectTranspilers) or invents fields — errors that silently break every later build.

data.Description: Add the Explainer DAG to any Effortless project — a generated, embedded visualization of the rulebook's calculated-field DAG that lets a user click any cell/field and see exactly how it was derived (raw inputs → lookups → calcs → aggregations), with RuleSpeak prose baked in at transpile time. Portable (vanilla JS + CSS) across React, Vue, plain HTML, Flask/Jinja, HTMX.
data.WhyItExists: A calculated field's provenance is otherwise invisible to the end user — they see the number, not the formula chain that produced it. This skill makes that chain inspectable in-app, on demand, without hand-building a DAG viewer per project.

data.Description: Best-practice dev-ops for an ERB project: a rulebook-first pipeline promoted across up to four tiers (dev/staging on localhost, beta/production on a live remote server), governed by one migration ledger, a derived (never stored) version, and two independent axes (DB migration version + code build). Ships a Deployment Management console, environment/DB switcher, and guardrails keeping staging/production reachable only through ledger-tracked migrations.
data.WhyItExists: Without a formal promotion model, 'push this rulebook change to production' has no safe, repeatable answer — dev/staging/prod drift silently. This skill is the one-time-per-project scaffold for a real release discipline.

data.Description: The exact, supported, scripted path to publish/push/deploy a new version of a transpiler tool in Versioned-Stable-SSoTme-Tools: scripts/publish-tool.sh <transpilerId> <category>/<tool-name>. Mirrors the green Deploy button in the transpiler-server UI. Distinct from `effortless build` (consumes a published tool) and from building the cpln workload alone (doesn't flip [latest] live).
data.WhyItExists: There is exactly one supported publish sequence; without this skill Claude invents a plausible-looking but wrong one (hand-rolled cpln apply, skipping the version-flip step) that leaves [latest] stale.

data.Description: Launch a self-rebuilding Docker stack (Postgres + generated API + generated Vite UI) that views and partially edits an effortless-rulebook.json in the browser.
data.WhyItExists: Users want a one-command way to open the rulebook editor and have it just work, rather than hand-rolling Docker/Postgres wiring per project. Name/Description/_meta are genuinely editable today; everything else stays view-only until the write-back roadmap grows.

data.Description: Add a general-purpose __meta__ table to a rulebook for global name/value settings, phrase atoms, and thresholds that don't belong to any domain entity — deliberately ignored by every transpiler.
data.WhyItExists: Projects kept inventing ad-hoc places for global config/reusable phrases, sometimes confusing it with the _meta conversion-metadata section. This skill gives one canonical, transpiler-ignored home for that class of data and explains why the double-underscore naming matters.

data.Description: Produce narrated explainer videos about Effortless/CMCC concepts or rulebooks, where the video itself is authored as a rulebook (Storyboards/Acts/Scenes/Clips/Assets) in the effortless-vid-01-full-name producer repo.
data.WhyItExists: The video producer practices what ERB preaches — one rulebook drives the whole video (script, timing, assets) instead of hand-editing scripts/render code per video. This skill prevents the single worst mistake already made once: editing generated rendering code instead of the rulebook to change the story.

data.Description: `effortless-rulebook.json` is the single source of truth for an ERB project; every other artifact is derived from it.
A surface that writes changes into the hub — rulebook-direct edit (the default), hand-edit with permission, Airtable, or reverse-sync.
A substrate mechanically regenerated from the hub (Postgres, Go, Python, docs, RuleSpeak, etc.) that must never be hand-edited to persist a change.
The best-practice default: edit the hub JSON directly rather than through an upstream grid like Airtable.
The privileged combination: an LLM tends the JSON hub directly and `effortless build` projects it to Postgres.
The agent's own posture inside ERB — it edits the hub and customization seams, never generated output.
Any execution target the rulebook is projected into (Postgres, Go, Python, XLSX, OWL, COBOL, ARM64, English...).
The claim that all substrates are interchangeable projections of the same rulebook, none privileged.
Editing the hub directly, then pushing the change back out to an upstream surface like Airtable to keep it mirrored.
Airtable is one sibling editing surface (like Excel/Notion), never the SSoT, and only relevant if a project explicitly opted in.
The rulebook's tables and FK relationships form a Directed Acyclic Graph — no cycles, no many-to-many.
Many-to-many relationships are forbidden; they must be modeled via a first-class junction entity.
Tables are PascalCase, plural, no underscores or symbols.
A calculated display/logical-key field, always the first field on a table, formed from a formula over other fields.

A foreign key field on the child (many) side uses the SINGULAR entity name with NO "Id" suffix — e.g. `Order.Customer` (FK to `Customers`), `Employee.Role` (FK to `Roles`), never `Order.CustomerId`. The field's stored value is the parent's `<Entity>Id` value (e.g. the slug "acme-corp"), and lookups always MATCH on `<Entity>Id`, never on `Name` (`=INDEX(Customers!{{Region}}, MATCH({{Customer}}, Customers!{{CustomerId}}, 0))`). The reverse relationship on the parent side uses the PLURAL name (`Customer.Orders`, `Role.Employees`) and is always 1-to-many, with the singular side as parent and the plural side as children. This pattern also enforces the DAG's no-many-to-many rule: a many-to-many need is expressed as two 1-to-many FKs through a junction table (e.g. `Enrollment.Student` + `Enrollment.Course`).
Within a table, calculated fields are ordered in levels (raw, then 1st-order, then 2nd-order, etc.) by dependency.
The five kinds of rulebook fields: raw, calculated, lookup, relationship, aggregation.
The Excel-dialect formula language used for calculated/lookup/aggregation fields (`={{Field}}`, INDEX/MATCH, SUMIFS, etc.).
Every table and field must carry a Description — the semantic backbone of the DAG and generated docs.
The Conceptual Model Completeness Conjecture: any crisp conceptual model decomposes into SDLAF over a bitemporal ACID DAG.
The five primitives — Schema, Data, Lookups, Aggregations, Formulas — that any design-time semantics decomposes into.
Every fact carries both transaction time and valid time, making audit and 'what did we believe when' first-class.
The combination of ACID transactions, bitemporal storage, and a cycle-free DAG that CMCC requires.
The conjecture invites anyone to produce one sentence of design-time semantics that can't decompose into SDLAF.
The scannable list of code shapes (JOINs, recomputed aggregates, hand ORM models, etc.) that violate CMCC and their rulebook-shaped fix.
The order for handling an apparent rulebook limitation: re-shape as SDLAF, use a customization seam, then flag a missing primitive.
The instruction to answer 'is ERB good / could it model X' from inside the CMCC conjecture, not as a neutral outside critic.
Coding without the rulebook — hand-writing every schema/migration/DTO/serializer layer instead of generating from one hub.

The open transpiler registry protocol behind Effortless (github.com/SSoTme). The effortless CLI (aka ssotme/aicapture/aic) is its local driver — it clones, registers, and runs transpilers per effortless.json. A transpiler is one artifact-in -> one artifact-out unit, registered (via `effortless -install`), not bundled into the CLI itself.
A tool that consumes one well-defined input artifact and produces one well-defined output artifact.
The project's build-pipeline config file: ProjectSettings + ProjectTranspilers, generated/maintained by the CLI.
The array in effortless.json recording each registered transpiler's RelativePath, CommandLine, and IsDisabled state.
The atomic, deterministic command that runs every enabled transpiler and regenerates all output spokes from the hub.
The build flag that includes normally-disabled transpilers (used for reverse-sync to Airtable).
`effortless -install` is cwd-sensitive; you must cd into the target output directory before installing a transpiler.
Comparing every substrate's computed output against a shared answer-key.json to prove multi-substrate equivalence.
Local-dev Postgres (drop+recreate via init-db.sh) vs Bases (delta migrations via apply-migration.sh) — only one uses migrations.
The rulebook always lives at /effortless-rulebook/effortless-rulebook.json, never the project root.
The rulebook JSON is the fixed interchange format every transpiler must respect; no transpiler may change its shape.

Every table gets a generated `vw_<table_name>` view (in `03-create-views.sql`) that SELECTs all raw columns from the base table plus every calculated/lookup/aggregation field via `calc_*()` function calls, using `WITH (security_invoker = ON)`. ALWAYS read from `vw_*` views, NEVER from base tables — base tables only hold raw columns, and views aren't updatable in Postgres (they contain function-call columns), so INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE still target the base table while all SELECT/READ goes through the view. Cheapest way to inspect a view's fields is `psql -d <dbname> -c "\d vw_tablename"` (~zero context tokens) rather than catting `03-create-views.sql`. Also never JOIN one `vw_*` view onto another to pull a related entity's field — add a lookup field to the rulebook instead so the single view already contains it.
Generated Postgres tables holding only raw columns; the only correct write surface (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE).
The numbered SQL files (bootstrap, tables, functions, views, policies, data) rewritten by every build; never hand-edited.
The `*b-customize-*` files that run after generated SQL and persist across builds, for infrastructure the hub can't model.
A rulebook table pattern storing customization SQL rows keyed by CustomizationType, mapped to the `*b-customize-*` files.
Joining two vw_* views (or base tables) in app/SQL code instead of adding a lookup field to the rulebook.

Generated file `02-create-functions.sql` emits one `get_{table}_{field}(p_{pk} TEXT)` function per raw field (single-row retrieval) and one `calc_{table}_{field}(p_{pk} TEXT)` function per calculated/lookup/aggregation field — a 1:1 mapping with the rulebook's field definitions. All are `LANGUAGE plpgsql STABLE SECURITY DEFINER`. A lookup's `calc_*` function resolves the FK and selects a field from the related table (e.g. `calc_workflow_steps_assigned_role_label`); an aggregation's `calc_*` function counts or sums related rows (e.g. `calc_workflows_count_of_workflow_steps`). The `03-create-views.sql` layer then calls these functions as computed columns in `vw_*`, so lookups compose — a lookup can target another table's own `calc_*` field. Like all files 00-05, this file is regenerated by every `effortless build`; don't hand-edit it — change the rulebook field definition instead.

The script `rulebook-to-postgres` generates alongside the `0*.sql` files that DROPS and RECREATES the local Postgres DB from scratch on every run — there is no `migrations/` folder or incremental deltas for local-dev projects. It ships with a generic default (`DEFAULT_CONN=postgresql://postgres@localhost:5432/demo` and header `# demo - Database Initialization Script`) that setup MUST patch to the project's real DB name before the first run, and re-patch after any future regeneration, or `./init-db.sh` with no `DATABASE_URL` set will silently drop the wrong `demo` DB. Register it as a build step via `effortless -install -exec ./init-db.sh` (run from `/postgres/`) so `effortless build` runs it automatically as step 3 of the pipeline (refresh rulebook → regenerate SQL → drop/re-init DB via init-db.sh); if that install hits the `startIndex` registration bug, add the exec entry to `effortless.json` by hand with `CommandLine: "-exec ./init-db.sh"` (never prefix with `bash`/`sh`). The single exception is `bases.effortlessapi.com`-hosted DBs, which can't be dropped and instead use `postgres/apply-migration.sh`.
Local-dev Postgres has no migrations folder or tracking table; schema changes go through the rulebook + build, never ALTER TABLE.

The root cause of most "bugs" in an ERB project: a rule exists in the hub (effortless-rulebook.json) but a generated spoke hasn't been rebuilt to match, or app code has fallen out of sync with the view it consumes. Diagnose it cheapest-first: (1) validate the rulebook's DAG for broken FK targets — parse effortless-rulebook.json and flag any relationship field whose RelatedTo isn't a known table; (2) scan generated code for JOIN anti-patterns (`grep -r "JOIN" cmd/api/*.go` should be ~0) and base-table reads (`grep -rE "FROM (bids|rfps|companies|contacts|documents)\s" cmd/api/*.go` should mostly be INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, not SELECT) versus view usage (`grep -r "FROM vw_" cmd/api/*.go` should be high). When fixing drift found in app code, never patch the app to recompute a missing field — extend the hub so the field appears in the next build's view, since patching duplicates the rule instead of fixing the source of truth.
The core CHANGE-RULE → BUILD → CONSUME-VIEWS iterative cycle that makes ERB feel effortless.
The rule that Claude must ask the user before modifying the hub or running effortless build.
Check git status --porcelain before building, and never auto-commit build output on the user's behalf.
The routing logic for where a given kind of change (entity, scalar field, formula, CRUD) should be made.
The canonical rule: never read the full rulebook or generated SQL into context; query it with targeted one-liners instead.
The derived-file reading order (read-me-1st.txt → schema.min.json → schema.json → full rulebook → data.json) that avoids reading the full hub.
Because the DAG is explicit in the rulebook, isolated schema/formula tasks can be safely delegated to cold-start sub-agents.
The Airtable AI escape hatch (Playwright-driven) used only for schema operations the REST API can't perform (formulas, lookups, rollups, new tables).
The Airtable formula convention that produces every ERB table's compound Name key.
The canonical lookup order for the Airtable base id and API key across env var, ssotme.key, and effortless.json.
The input-spoke transpiler that pulls Airtable schema/data into the hub, only present when a project opted in.
The reverse-sync output transpiler that mirrors hub changes back to Airtable; stays disabled by default.
The plain-English rules document (definitional rules, vocabulary, fact types) generated from the rulebook by default.

In the RuleSpeak document generated by `rulebook-to-rulespeak`, every calculated, lookup, or aggregation field in the rulebook becomes one `DR-n` row under the "Definitional Rules" section — a plain-English restatement of that field's formula. The companion "Traceability to Schema" section maps each derived field back to its formula in `effortless-rulebook.json` (the hub SSoT), so a reader can go from English rule to exact source formula. Definitional rules are distinct from "Operative Rules" (structural must/must-not/should statements from schema flags like `nullable:false` or the optional `Constraints` table) — DR-n covers derivation logic, not obligations. This output is regenerated on every `effortless build` into `rulespeak/rulespeak.md` and `rulespeak/rulespeak.html`; never hand-edit it.
An in-app, generated visualization letting users click a derived cell and see its full field-provenance chain.
The HTML attribute (Table.Field) used to mark a derived display cell for Explainer DAG enhancement.

ExplainDAG is a generated *trace of reasoning*, not a generated program: for every derived value it records (1) which rule fired to produce it, (2) what witnesses — input rows, lookup targets, intermediate calculations — the rule consumed, and (3) what those witnesses in turn derive from, recursively down to raw data. This turns "why is this number what it is?" from archaeology (git blame, log spelunking, reconstructing intent from execution paths) into a query against a static artifact, making audit/regulation/reversibility first-class and giving downstream LLMs hallucination defense (a model shown the ExplainDAG alongside a derived value can't quietly assert a different derivation). It is ERB's bitemporal-ACID-DAG substrate's audit story made physical — provenance most codebases throw away is instead kept, because the CMCC conjecture says it is recoverable from the model. In the effortless-rulebooks repo it is one of the 11+ conformance-tested substrates generated from the same effortless-rulebook.json against answer-key.json, and the source SKILL.md names it as the substrate its author would "point at first."
A passwordless email-code JWT issuer that verifies 'this email holder proved it' and nothing more — no user store.
The auth.trusted_tenants table in a consuming app's Postgres, registering a magic-links tenant's public key for JWT verification.
SQL functions (jwt_email, jwt_claims, jwt_tenant_id, has_role) that let RLS policies read the verified JWT.

Postgres RLS policies filter rows by the JWT-verified identity, but must call the `app.jwt_*()` helper functions (`app.jwt_email()`, `app.jwt_tenant_id()`, `app.has_role('admin')`) — never `current_setting(...)` directly, since the helpers fail closed when no JWT has been set. Standard pattern: `ALTER TABLE x ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;` then a default-deny policy (`USING (false)`) followed by scoped policies such as `USING (owner_email = app.jwt_email())` for owner-only access and `USING (app.has_role('admin'))` for elevated roles. Before policies can read anything, each request must run `SELECT auth.set_jwt($1)` (the raw bearer token) inside a transaction — this RS256-verifies the token against `auth.trusted_tenants` and writes `app.jwt_*` values as transaction-local GUCs, so a pooled connection can never leak identity to the next request. Smoke-test with a real token wrapped in `BEGIN;`/`COMMIT;` (GUCs evaporate between statements outside a transaction) — e.g. `SELECT auth.set_jwt('<token>'); SELECT app.jwt_email(), app.jwt_tenant_id(), app.has_role('admin'); SET LOCAL ROLE app_anon; SELECT count(*) FROM documents;`. Avoid the v1 anti-pattern of `set_config('app.jwt_email', $1, true)` from app code, which lets RLS fire but trusts unverified app-supplied claims instead of a verified token.
The hosted Postgres platform (bases.effortlessapi.com) — the one ERB deployment shape that uses migrations because its DB is live/shared.
The single, append-only record (folders on disk + each environment's schema_migrations) that is the sole authority for a tier's DB version.
The rule that a tier's 'version' is always computed from the migration ledger on read, never stored as a separate authority.
DB migration version and code build are tracked and promoted separately per environment tier.
The admin console showing the migration x environment matrix, drift grading, and the full promotion action rail.
The rule that dev >= staging >= beta >= production always; any violation is surfaced loudly.
The up-to-four-tier promotion chain (dev/staging/beta/production), where only dev is drop+reseeded and the rest move by migration only.
The one-time, idempotent migration capturing the entire init-db schema stack so any tier can be built from nothing.
The local driver binary (effortless, aka ssotme/aicapture/aic) that clones/registers/runs transpilers per effortless.json.
The two GitHub orgs: SSoTme (foundational tooling/protocol) and effortlessapi (methodology, rulebooks, this skill set).
The empirical demonstration repo: one rulebook projected into 11+ substrates, conformance-tested against an answer key.
The always-on Model Context Protocol endpoint exposing the transpiler catalog and skill set as tools/resources to any MCP client.

data.ConceptLabel: Skill Set SSoT vs Installed Copies
data.Description: The distinction between the git-tracked skills/ clone (edit here) and the runtime copies under ~/.claude/skills/.

The one supported scripted path for publishing a new version of a transpiler tool in `Versioned-Stable-SSoTme-Tools`, mirroring the green Deploy button in the transpiler-server UI. Usage: `API_BASE="http://localhost:<PORT>/api" ./scripts/publish-tool.sh <transpilerId> <category>/<tool-name>` (e.g. `recyxbCdc8WlhTTfs effortless/rulebook-to-sql-server`). It drives `GET /api/transpilers/:transpilerId/deploy/stream?toolPath=...&steps=airtable,metadata,build,wait` to create the Airtable `TranspilerVersions` record, copy metadata, generate a `yyyy.mm.dd.hhmm` version, build+push the Docker image via `build-and-push-cpln-workload.sh`, `cpln apply` to GVC `ssotme-tools`, and wait online — then on SSE `complete` calls `PUT /api/versions/:versionRecordId {"IsActive": true}` to flip `[latest]` live. Unlike `build-and-push-cpln-workload.sh` alone (build+push only, does not flip `[latest]`) or `effortless build`/`-install` (which only consumes an already-published tool), this is the only script that actually publishes. Requires `cpln` CLI authenticated, `jq`, and the transpiler-server running (find its port with `ps aux | grep transpiler-server` + `lsof` if not on the default `localhost:3000`) — never hand-roll `cpln apply` + manual Deploy-click, and never POST to `/api/transpilers/:id/deploy` (deleted, produced broken un-built records).
Each Effortless app hard-codes a random odd port for the API at scaffold time, with the SPA port fixed at API_PORT+1, baked into start.sh and never changed afterward.

Every Effortless app project's `start.sh` must follow a fixed contract. Pick one random odd port at scaffold time (e.g. `8731`) and hard-code it as `API_PORT`; the SPA/client port is always `API_PORT + 1` (the next even number), hard-coded in `start.sh`, `server/src/index.ts` (or `PORT` default), and `web/vite.config.ts` (proxy target + `server.port`) — never reuse generic defaults like `3000` or `5173`. `./start.sh` with no arguments must be the only way to run the app: it kills anything bound to `API_PORT`/`UI_PORT` (`lsof -ti tcp:<port> | xargs kill -9`), restarts the API and SPA dev servers, and prints clickable `http://localhost:<port>` lines for both. Only non-run subcommands are allowed (`build` → `effortless build`, `db` → `init-db.sh`) — do not add `all`, `server`, or `web` subcommands. Pick `API_PORT` randomly from 3001–9999 at scaffold time and never change it after the first commit.

Step 4 of effortless-init: write a project-root CLAUDE.md from the standard template, filling in {ProjectName} and {baseId} -- "without this, future Claude sessions break the methodology." It must encode the 8 CRITICAL RULES (rulebook is SSoT; never edit generated postgres/00-05 files; read from vw_* views but write to base tables; query the rulebook via targeted Python one-liners instead of Read/cat-ing the whole JSON; ask permission before rulebook edits or effortless build; always run effortless build after hub changes; never reimplement business logic in app code; no migrations on local Postgres -- edit the rulebook and rebuild instead, except bases-hosted DBs), plus sections for Editing the Hub, Airtable Base (if connected), The Effortless Loop, Build and Start, RuleSpeak, ERB Skills routing, and a "Posture on the methodology itself" section instructing the agent to load effortless-cmcc before answering evaluative questions about ERB rather than defaulting to generic "balanced reviewer" LLM priors.
.ssotme/ is per-machine CLI scratch state (caches, transient build artifacts, key references) that must be gitignored on every effortless -init and never committed.
The transpiler that reads a populated rulebook-export.json and produces an Excel workbook, one sheet per entity including calculated/aggregated columns.
Server code invoking the effortless CLI (or any transpiler) as a subprocess must use async spawn, never execSync, because execSync blocks the Node event loop.

To export live DB data through a transpiler that only understands the rulebook JSON shape, stage the data by loading `effortless-rulebook.json`, clearing every table's `data` array (keeping the schema), then querying each `vw_*` view in Postgres and repopulating `data` with the live rows — mapping each view's snake_case columns back to the rulebook's PascalCase field names (e.g. `field.name.replace(/([A-Z])/g, '_$1').toLowerCase().replace(/^_/, '')`). Write the populated result to `rulebook-export.json` in the project root, then run the transpiler against it (e.g. `effortless rulebook-to-xlsx -i ./rulebook-export.json -o {project-name}-rulebook.xlsx`) via `spawn` (never `execSync`, which blocks the event loop). Reading from `vw_*` views rather than base tables means calculated, lookup, and aggregation columns are included automatically. After streaming the output file back to the client, delete both the generated output file and the temporary `rulebook-export.json`.
Guidance for authoring SKILL.md files: description as trigger-spec not summary, ~150-line target, lead with rules not tutorial framing, link instead of restate.

To deprecate a skill, add an entry to `<clone>/DEPRECATED_SKILLS.md` — `install.sh` parses this table on every run to clean up users' installed copies (removing the corresponding `~/.claude/skills/effortless-*` directory). Optionally leave a shim `SKILL.md` in `skills/<old-name>/` that points to the replacement skill until the target removal date, so users mid-transition still get guidance instead of a dead load.
The MCP server bakes a frozen copy of the transpiler catalog and the effortless-claude skills at image build time; local dev reads live instead.
The T-SQL counterpart to rulebook-to-postgres — same 00-05 file numbering, calc_* functions, vw_* views, RLS via security policies, driven by init-db.sh via sqlcmd instead of psql.
When moving a project from one execution substrate to another, the old substrate's DB-init transpiler/build-step entries must be explicitly disabled so only one active DB init runs per build.
The local Node service that drives transpiler versioning, deploys, and the Airtable TranspilerVersions bookkeeping — the backend behind both the Deploy button and publish-tool.sh.
Control Plane workloads scale to zero; the first request after a publish or long idle hits a cold start and can time out — hit /healthz first before assuming a fresh deploy is broken.

Always install the `effortless` CLI under the same Node version the user's generated apps will run on — the CLI itself runs on Node 16+, but generated apps (Vite 5) require Node 18+ since `crypto.getRandomValues` is missing on Node 16. If the Node version differs, `which effortless` can resolve to a different nvm prefix and switching versions silently "loses" the CLI. Symptoms it's needed: `crypto.getRandomValues is not a function`, ESM `node:` import errors, or "this worked a few days ago" after an nvm change — check `node --version` before suggesting "downgrade Vite." Fix: `nvm install 20 || true; nvm use 20 && nvm alias default 20; cd ~/.effortless/cli && npm install -g .`; rebuild any app's `node_modules` built against Node 16 with `rm -rf node_modules package-lock.json && npm install`. Note `nvm alias default 20` only affects new shells, so bake a version-check/switch into `start.sh` for existing projects.
Older machines may have a legacy PKG-installed ssotme/aicapture at /usr/local/bin; the npm-based install doesn't remove them, so PATH ordering determines which copy wins.
A minimizerulebook transpiler emits progressively higher-fidelity derived files beside the rulebook (read-me-1st.txt, schema.min.json, schema.json, data.json) for cheap querying.
Any time an agent authors or first populates a rulebook hub, installing rulebook-to-rulespeak and running a build is mandatory before handing work back.

For deontic rules beyond plain schema flags like `nullable:false`, add a `Constraints` table to the rulebook. Each row points at a boolean calculated field on an entity and annotates it with one of `MustBeTrue` / `MustNotBeTrue` / `ShouldBeTrue`, which `rulebook-to-rulespeak` renders into the RuleSpeak document's Operative Rules section as structural `must` / `must not` / `should` prose. See the `rulebook-to-rulespeak` tool README (`UsingRulespeakConstraints.md`) for the full column contract.
Any derived (calculated/lookup/aggregation) display value in the host app is wrapped with data-er-dag="Table.Field"; raw editable inputs and FK displays are never wrapped.
The explainer DAG's five routing modes (callback, path, hash, modal, htmx) determine how the generated JS integrates with the host's own router or lack thereof.
For transpiler-driven UI features like the explainer DAG, the transpiler output itself is the UI — the host only mounts static assets; hand-rolling equivalents is forbidden.

The 11-step bootstrap pipeline (word extraction, vocabulary, glossary, narrative, mock data, normalized schema, rulebook, descriptions, seed data, DAG extension, enter the loop) turning raw requirements into a rulebook.
The transpiler that generates a rough, not-guaranteed-internally-consistent starting rulebook from a requirements text file — a bootstrap starting point, not a production artifact.
Client-facing README/glossary/narrative material must lead with what the system does, not how it's built — rulebook/DAG/ERB infrastructure belongs in dev docs, not user materials.

Most "bugs" in an ERB project are hub/spoke drift, not real defects: either a rule exists in the hub but a generated spoke hasn't been rebuilt to match, or app code has gone stale relative to the view it consumes. The diagnostic posture is to spot that drift state without assigning blame, starting with the cheapest check first — query the rulebook itself (e.g. validate the DAG for broken FK targets by checking every `relationship` field's `RelatedTo` against the set of known tables) before inspecting generated code (grep for JOIN anti-patterns, base-table reads vs `vw_*` view reads). When a diagnostic finds a missing field, the fix is to extend the hub so it appears in the next build's view, not to patch the app to recompute it — patching the app duplicates the rule and reintroduces the same class of drift.
OMNI can be driven either human-in-the-loop (generating prompt files for the user to paste manually) or Playwright-automated (omni-send.mjs driving a headed Chrome session).

Before running `~/.claude/skills/effortless-airtable-omni/omni-send.mjs` (Playwright-driven OMNI automation), verify: (1) Node 18+ on PATH; (2) Playwright + Chromium installed, preferably project-local via `npx playwright --version || { npm install -D playwright && npx playwright install chromium; }`; (3) a headed display — the script launches Chrome headed on purpose and will fail/hang on headless servers/CI; (4) a persistent profile dir (default `/tmp/airtable-omni-profile`) that survives across runs after first manual login — never delete it unless the user asks to log out; (5) network access to airtable.com (the script navigates to `https://airtable.com/<baseId>` and times out with a debug screenshot if blocked); (6) a valid Airtable base id, pulled via `cat effortless.json | jq -r '.ProjectSettings[] | select(.Name == "baseId") | .Value'`. If any prerequisite is missing, stop and tell the user before running the script — OMNI failures with broken prerequisites usually waste an entire debug cycle.

After a request's bearer token is validated via `SELECT auth.set_jwt($1)` inside a transaction, RLS policies must read identity through the `app.jwt_*()` helper functions — never `current_setting(...)` directly. Available helpers: `app.jwt_email()`, `app.jwt_tenant_id()`, `app.jwt_claims()`, and `app.has_role('admin')`. They read transaction-local GUCs that `auth.set_jwt()` populated after RS256-verifying the token against `auth.trusted_tenants`, and they fail closed when no JWT has been set. Example policy: `CREATE POLICY "owner_select" ON documents FOR SELECT TO magiclink_consumer USING (owner_email = app.jwt_email());`. Writing `app.jwt_email` directly from app code (`set_config('app.jwt_email', $1, true)`) is the v1 GUC-cache anti-pattern — the DB then trusts unverified input; migrate such code to call `auth.set_jwt($token)` and rewrite policies to use the helper. Caution: if a helper (e.g. `app.jwt_role()`) itself reads an RLS-protected table, it can trigger infinite recursion (`stack depth limit exceeded`) unless the resolver is `SECURITY DEFINER` with `SET row_security = off`.

The Effortless MCP server exposes `effortless://skills/*` resources from a frozen copy of `github.com/effortlessapi/effortless-claude/skills/` taken at image build time — not a live read of the repo. It also exposes ~54 MCP tools, one auto-generated per active transpiler in a similarly baked catalog snapshot, with schemas sourced from the Airtable Parameter table. Both snapshots are refreshed via explicit bake scripts (`./scripts/bake-catalog.sh` for the transpiler catalog, `./scripts/bake-skills.sh` for the skills folder) run before bumping the version and publishing through the transpiler-server UI. Local dev differs: it reads skills from the sibling `effortless-claude/skills/` repo directly (no bake step needed), so only the deployed image is actually frozen.

Before running `effortless build`, run `git status --porcelain` (read-only) to check the tree. If it's non-empty, pause and ask the user for permission to build — they may want to commit or stash first so the resulting diff cleanly isolates the build output. Do not offer to commit, stash, or `git add` anything yourself; the user owns their git state. Once the user gives the go-ahead (or the tree is already clean), proceed with the build.

`effortless-rulebook.json` is the IR (intermediate representation) and hub that every transpiler in the ssotme:// protocol reads from or writes to — it is the contract all transpilers must respect, and same rulebook in always yields same artifact out (determinism). Output spokes (postgres, xlsx, docs, airtable reverse-sync) read it as input; input spokes (LLM direct edits — the default — plus optional raw-text-to-rulebook, airtable-to-rulebook) write it as output. No transpiler may change the IR's shape: if a transpiler needs more data, add fields to the rulebook itself, not to `effortless.json` (the separate config file that only registers which transpilers run, via `ProjectTranspilers`). Referenced via `-i ../effortless-rulebook/effortless-rulebook.json` in a transpiler's `CommandLine`.

`EffortlessExplainer.init({...})` takes a `mode` option choosing how DAG pages navigate: `callback` for React/Vue/Svelte SPAs (host router owns URLs, requires a `routing: { navigate, navigateTable, fieldHref, tableHref, onBack, onHome }` object); `path` for multi-page/server-rendered apps with full reloads; `hash` for static sites with zero server routing (`#/dag/Table/Field`); `modal` for HTMX/Jinja apps (overlay, URL unchanged); and `htmx` which sets an `htmxFieldUrl` template for HTMX navigation. Common options across modes include `mountToggle` (selector for the ƒ-glyph on/off toggle, persisted in `localStorage`) and `enhance: false` in SPAs, where the host calls `enhanceCells()` itself after render instead of relying on the one-time DOM scan. Pitfall: using `path` mode inside an SPA with a client router breaks re-rendering on navigation (no `popstate` listener) — SPAs must use `callback` mode with `renderFieldPage`/`renderTablePage`/`renderTablesIndex` route components instead.

`effortless build -id` (include disabled) forces execution of ALL registered transpilers, even those marked `"IsDisabled": true` in `effortless.json` — whereas plain `effortless build` skips disabled ones. This is essential for reverse-sync: `rulebook-to-airtable` is normally installed with `IsDisabled: true` in `push-to-airtable/` so it never runs on a regular build, and is only invoked deliberately via `cd effortless-rulebook/push-to-airtable/ && effortless build -id` to mirror hub edits back to Airtable.

Older Macs may have `/usr/local/bin/{ssotme,aicapture}` left over from the old PKG installer; the npm install of the `effortless` CLI does not touch or remove those — it places its own symlinks in the npm global prefix instead. Whichever bin dir comes first on `PATH` wins, so if `/usr/local/bin` resolves before the npm/nvm prefix, `which effortless`/`which ssotme` can silently run the stale legacy binary. Diagnose with `echo $PATH | tr ':' '\n' | grep -nE 'nvm|/usr/local/bin'` and `which -a effortless ssotme`; fix by reordering PATH so the npm prefix wins, or (only with explicit user confirmation) removing the legacy symlinks via `sudo rm /usr/local/bin/ssotme /usr/local/bin/aicapture`.

`effortless-rulebook.json` always lives at `/effortless-rulebook/effortless-rulebook.json` — NEVER at the project root. Before running `effortless airtable-to-rulebook` or `effortless -install airtable-to-rulebook`, `cd effortless-rulebook` first; running from the root dumps the rulebook in the wrong place and poisons every subsequent build. If `effortless-rulebook.json` ever appears at the project root, it's a bug: delete it, fix `effortless.json` so `airtable-to-rulebook` has `RelativePath: /effortless-rulebook`, and redo the install from inside `/effortless-rulebook/`.

data.ConceptLabel: Port Convention (Odd API, Even API+1 SPA)
data.Description: Every Effortless app project picks one random odd port for the API at scaffold time (e.g. 8731) and hard-codes it in start.sh — never reuse generic defaults like 3000, 5173, or 6164. The SPA/client port is always API_PORT + 1 (the next even number, e.g. 8732); hard-code both in start.sh, server/src/index.ts (or the PORT default), and web/vite.config.ts (proxy target + server.port). Pick API_PORT from a random odd number in the 3001-9999 range at scaffold time and never change it after the first commit. `./start.sh` with no arguments must kill anything already bound to both ports (`lsof -ti tcp:<port> | xargs kill -9`), restart both dev servers, and print clickable http://localhost:<port> lines for both.

Every Effortless project must gitignore CLI scratch state: create (or append to) `.gitignore` in the project root with the single entry `.ssotme/`. `.ssotme/` is per-machine CLI working state (caches, transient build artifacts, key references) — it is never source and must never be committed. Add this on every `effortless -init`, before the first commit.

ConceptSkills.Description: Junction table: which skill(s) each Concept is most central to. A many-to-many between Concepts and Skills modeled as two 1-to-many FKs, per ERB DAG conventions.

schema.name: Name
schema.Description: Logical PK — Concept + Skill composite.

schema.name: Concept
schema.Description: The concept.

schema.name: Skill
schema.Description: The skill this concept is most central to.

Gotchas.Description: Specific anti-patterns per skill — what the plausible-but-wrong approach looks like and what the actual fix is. Extracted from each SKILL.md's explicit warnings; distinct from Concepts (definitions) — these are traps.

schema.name: Name
schema.Description: Logical PK — kebab-cased GotchaKey.

schema.name: GotchaKey
schema.Description: Skill-scoped unique key (Skill::title-slug) supplied at extraction time.

schema.name: Title
schema.Description: Short name for the trap.

schema.name: LooksRight
schema.Description: The plausible-but-wrong approach — what someone would naively try.

schema.name: ActualFix
schema.Description: What is actually correct, and why the naive approach fails.

schema.name: Severity
schema.Description: critical = silent data corruption, security hole, or breaks the core methodology guarantee; moderate = a bug or wasted work but locally contained.

schema.name: GotchaSkills
schema.Description: Join rows linking this gotcha to the skill(s) it applies to.

data.Title: Editing generated 00-05 SQL / output files instead of the rulebook
data.LooksRight: Opening a generated Postgres file (00-05 in postgres/) or other output-spoke file (generated Python/Go/docs) and patching it directly when it 'looks wrong', since that's the file that actually runs.
data.ActualFix: Never edit generated files — they're mechanical output rewritten on every `effortless build`. Trace back to the rulebook entry that produced the wrong output and fix it there; patching the artifact directly is at best temporary. The hub (`effortless-rulebook.json`, directly or via an input spoke) and the `*b-customize-*` customization seams are the only places work persists.

data.Title: Reading base tables instead of vw_* views (or writing to views)
data.LooksRight: Querying a base table directly to get a 'calculated' or 'lookup' field value, or trying to write/UPDATE a vw_* view because it has the convenient joined/calculated columns.
data.ActualFix: Always read from `vw_*` views (they include calculated/lookup/aggregation fields) and always write to base tables directly — the views aren't updatable anyway.

data.Title: Writing a SQL migration / ALTER TABLE on local-dev
data.LooksRight: Reaching for `ALTER TABLE`, a `migrations/` folder, or a migrations-tracking log entry to make a schema change on the local Postgres instance.
data.ActualFix: Local Postgres is regenerated from scratch by `init-db.sh` on every build — there is no migrations folder or tracking table there. Schema changes go through the rulebook (edit the JSON, or via Airtable if connected) → `effortless build`. The only exception is `bases.effortlessapi.com`-hosted DBs, which use `postgres/apply-migration.sh` because the DB can't be dropped — and even there, schema still originates in the rulebook.

data.Title: Writing imperative business logic instead of a Lookup/Aggregation/Formula
data.LooksRight: Implementing a business rule as procedural/imperative code (in the app layer or a script) when it 'feels like real logic' that doesn't belong in a declarative JSON schema.
data.ActualFix: First ask whether it's actually a Lookup, Aggregation, or Formula in disguise — usually yes. If it genuinely doesn't fit, use a customization seam (`*b-customize-*` files / `ERBCustomizations` table) with a comment explaining why the rulebook can't express the rule, rather than dropping to imperative logic that breaks substrate-equivalence.

data.Title: Running airtable-to-rulebook install/build from the project root
data.LooksRight: Running `effortless airtable-to-rulebook` or `effortless -install airtable-to-rulebook` from the project root directory, since that's the 'normal' place to run CLI commands.
data.ActualFix: Must `cd effortless-rulebook` first — `effortless-rulebook.json` always lives at `/effortless-rulebook/effortless-rulebook.json`, never at project root. Running from root dumps the rulebook in the wrong place and poisons every subsequent build. If it appears at the root, delete it, fix `effortless.json`'s `RelativePath`, and redo the install from inside `/effortless-rulebook/`.

data.Title: Reading effortless-rulebook.json directly / using query_rulebook MCP tool to inspect schema
data.LooksRight: Calling `Read`/`cat` on the full `effortless-rulebook.json` file to 'check' the schema, or using the `query_rulebook` MCP tool as the first move to query it — both seem like the direct, obvious way to inspect the hub.
data.ActualFix: Never read the full rulebook directly — it can be megabytes and floods context, defeating the point of a structured rulebook. Never use `query_rulebook` MCP tool as a first move either — it's a network round-trip, no better than a local one-liner. Use targeted `effortless-query` Python one-liners (or the `minimize-rulebook` derived ladder — read-me-1st.txt → schema.min.json → schema.json → full → derived-data.json) to extract only the needed table/field metadata.

data.Title: Reading generated files after a build to 'verify' them
data.LooksRight: After running `effortless build`, opening/catting the generated SQL or output files to confirm the build did the right thing.
data.ActualFix: `effortless build` is a zero-context, deterministic operation — you don't need to read the output. The pattern is: determine something changed → build → commit → done. Trust the pipeline; you already knew the schema before the build because you queried it.

data.Title: Editing the rulebook JSON without asking permission
data.LooksRight: Directly modifying `effortless-rulebook.json` because you're confident it's the right change and it's faster than pausing to ask.
data.ActualFix: Always ask permission before modifying the rulebook JSON directly — it's the SSoT, and the developer should be choosing when it changes.

data.Title: Running `effortless build` as the final step during reverse-sync
data.LooksRight: Always ending a rulebook-touching workflow with `effortless build`, including when reverse-syncing rulebook → Airtable.
data.ActualFix: `effortless build` is usually the final step, EXCEPT when reverse-syncing rulebook → Airtable — building first would overwrite HEAD JSON before the push to Airtable completes.

data.Title: Reading generated Postgres files instead of the rulebook
data.LooksRight: Editing files 00-05 under postgres/ directly to change behavior, since they contain the actual SQL logic.
data.ActualFix: NEVER edit generated files — files 00-05 in postgres/ are regenerated on every build. The rulebook JSON is the source of truth; change it there and rerun `effortless build`.

data.Title: Reading base tables instead of vw_* views
data.LooksRight: Querying/reading application data straight from the base tables since that's where the raw rows live.
data.ActualFix: Always read from vw_* views, never base tables. Always WRITE to base tables directly (reads and writes go through different surfaces).

data.Title: Directly Read/cat-ing the whole rulebook JSON
data.LooksRight: Using Read or `cat effortless-rulebook/effortless-rulebook.json` to inspect the schema or a table's fields.
data.ActualFix: Query the rulebook first — never read it directly. The file can be megabytes; a full Read floods context and is never necessary. Use targeted python one-liners (or effortless-query) instead, and never reach for the query_rulebook MCP tool when a local one-liner does the job. Don't grep generated SQL either — the rulebook is the source.

data.Title: Reimplementing business logic in app code
data.LooksRight: Recomputing a derived value (e.g. a status flag or total) in application code because it's convenient or the view field isn't wired up yet.
data.ActualFix: Never reimplement business logic in app code — consume calculated fields from views as opaque truth.

data.Title: Writing migrations / ALTER TABLE against local Postgres
data.LooksRight: When a schema change is needed, writing an ALTER TABLE, adding a file to postgres/migrations/, or inserting into a migrations tracking table — the usual instinct for evolving a live DB.
data.ActualFix: NO MIGRATIONS on this project's local Postgres. `init-db.sh` drops + recreates the DB on every build — there is no migrations folder or tracking table. Never run ALTER TABLE against the live DB. The fix is always 'edit the rulebook (directly, or via Airtable) and rerun `effortless build`.' Bases-hosted DBs (bases.effortlessapi.com) are the lone exception.

data.Title: Installing the Airtable rulebook transpiler from the project root
data.LooksRight: Running `effortless -install airtable-to-rulebook -o effortless-rulebook.json -account airtable` from the project root, since that's where effortless.json lives.
data.ActualFix: This must be installed from inside `/effortless-rulebook/` — this is load-bearing (per the ORCHESTRATION RULE in effortless-orchestrator), not a stylistic preference.

data.Title: Modifying the rulebook or running a build without asking
data.LooksRight: Proactively editing the rulebook hub (directly or via Airtable/reverse-sync) or running `effortless build` as soon as a change seems needed, to save a round-trip.
data.ActualFix: Ask permission before modifying the rulebook via any input spoke or running `effortless build`.

data.Title: Reusing generic default ports for start.sh
data.LooksRight: Hard-coding common defaults like 3000, 5173, or 6164 for the API/SPA ports in start.sh.
data.ActualFix: Pick one random odd port at scaffold time and hard-code it; never reuse generic defaults. The SPA/client port must always be API_PORT + 1 (the next even number), hard-coded consistently in start.sh, server/src/index.ts, and web/vite.config.ts.

data.Title: Adding extra start.sh subcommands (all/server/web)
data.LooksRight: Adding convenience subcommands like `./start.sh server` or `./start.sh all` to run just the backend or everything explicitly.
data.ActualFix: Do not add all, server, or web subcommands — `./start.sh` alone (no arguments) is the only way to run the app; only `build` and `db` are allowed as optional subcommands.

data.Title: Building schema in Airtable first, then pulling into the rulebook
data.LooksRight: Start a new project by creating tables in Airtable via OMNI, adding descriptions/mock data through the Airtable REST API, extending the model with lookups/rollups in the grid, and finally running `airtable-to-rulebook` to pull it into the hub — treating Airtable as the place schema authoring begins.
data.ActualFix: This is explicitly labeled the 'legacy path' and 'no longer the recommended path.' The correct flow is Rulebook-First: author descriptions, mock data, and the full inference DAG directly in effortless-rulebook.json (Steps 8-11), since LLMs edit the rulebook natively with no round-trip needed. Airtable, if wanted at all, should be populated FROM the finished rulebook via `rulebook-to-airtable` (reverse-sync) as a downstream convenience, not a bootstrap step.

data.Title: Exposing ERB/rulebook infrastructure in user-facing docs
data.LooksRight: When writing the README, glossary, or narrative description for the client, describe how the system was built — mentioning the rulebook, calculated fields, DAG structure, and Airtable/Excel integration as selling points or explanatory detail.
data.ActualFix: The rulebook, DAG, and calculated-field machinery are implementation details that belong only in CLAUDE.md and developer guides. User-facing materials (glossaries, narratives, mockups) must lead with what the system does for the business, using domain vocabulary only — never the ERB/methodology internals.

data.Title: Treating raw-text-to-rulebook output as production-ready
data.LooksRight: Run `raw-text-to-rulebook` on requirements.txt, get bootstrap-rulebook.json, and start building/using it directly as the project's rulebook.
data.ActualFix: The transpiler output is explicitly 'a rough (not guaranteed internally consistent) starting-point' — it must be reviewed, normalized, and extended through the full Shadle steps (glossary, narrative, mock data, DAG layering, descriptions) before it becomes the production effortless-rulebook.json.

data.Title: Writing migrations / ALTER TABLE on local-dev Postgres
data.LooksRight: Schema needs to change, so you write an ALTER TABLE statement, create a postgres/migrations/ folder, or insert into a migrations/schema_migrations tracking table to apply the delta incrementally, like you would on a normal app database.
data.ActualFix: Local-dev DB is regenerate-from-scratch: init-db.sh drops and recreates the whole DB from freshly generated SQL on every `effortless build`. There is no migrations folder or tracking table for local-dev. Schema changes always go through editing the rulebook and rerunning `effortless build`. The only exception is bases.effortlessapi.com-hosted DBs, which use postgres/apply-migration.sh because they can't be dropped — and even there, schema still originates in the rulebook.

data.Title: Running `effortless airtable-to-rulebook` from the project root
data.LooksRight: You cd into the project root (where effortless.json lives) and run `effortless airtable-to-rulebook` / `effortless -install airtable-to-rulebook` directly, since that's the project's top-level working directory.
data.ActualFix: The rulebook must live at `/effortless-rulebook/effortless-rulebook.json`, not project root. Running from root dumps the file into the wrong place and registers the transpiler with RelativePath: '/', which poisons every subsequent `effortless build`. Always `cd effortless-rulebook && effortless -install airtable-to-rulebook -account airtable -o effortless-rulebook.json && cd ..`. If effortless-rulebook.json is ever found at project root, that's a bug to fix by deleting it and redoing the install from inside /effortless-rulebook/.

data.Title: Running `effortless -install` from the wrong directory for any transpiler
data.LooksRight: You run `effortless -install rulebook-to-postgres -i ./effortless-rulebook/effortless-rulebook.json` from the project root, assuming -install just needs the right -i input path and doesn't care about cwd.
data.ActualFix: `effortless -install` is cwd-sensitive: it writes output to whatever directory you run it from and registers that directory as the transpiler's RelativePath, which every future `effortless build` uses. You must `cd` into the target output folder (e.g. `postgres/`) BEFORE running -install. If SQL artifacts (0*.sql, init-db.sh, function-overrides/) show up at project root, the fix is to redo the install from the correct directory, not to manually move the files afterward.

data.Title: Leaving the transpiler's default DB name (`demo`) in init-db.sh
data.LooksRight: After installing rulebook-to-postgres, you just run ./init-db.sh right away — it's generated, so it must already be configured correctly for this project.
data.ActualFix: rulebook-to-postgres ships a generic DEFAULT_CONN pointing at a `demo` database with a `# demo - Database Initialization Script` header. If left in place, anyone running ./init-db.sh with no DATABASE_URL set will silently drop+recreate a `demo` DB unrelated to this project. This must be patched (both the header comment and DEFAULT_CONN line) to the real DB name before the first run, and reapplied after any future regeneration.

data.Title: Guessing the CommandLine shell-invocation form for -exec build steps
data.LooksRight: When manually registering init-db.sh as a build step, you write CommandLine as `"exec bash init-db.sh"` or `"bash init-db.sh"` or just `"./init-db.sh"`, treating the transpiler engine like it needs an explicit shell/interpreter prefix.
data.ActualFix: The runtime itself is the shell, so CommandLine must be exactly `-exec ./init-db.sh` — do not prepend bash, sh, cmd, or the word exec redundantly with a shell name. Wrong forms silently break the -exec step registration.

data.Title: Reading generated SQL / editing generated 0*.sql files to inspect or fix schema
data.LooksRight: To understand or tweak the schema you open and edit the generated postgres/0*.sql files directly, or read through them at length to 'verify' the build worked.
data.ActualFix: Never edit generated 0*.sql files — they get overwritten on the next build. To inspect schema, use lightweight zero-token-cost tools instead: `psql -c "\d vw_<table>"` or the effortless-query skill's one-liners against the rulebook JSON — not re-reading the full rulebook or generated SQL.

data.Title: Auto-committing or stashing on the user's behalf around `effortless build`
data.LooksRight: Before/after running `effortless build` on a dirty tree, you helpfully run `git add`/`git commit`/`git stash` yourself so the diff is clean or so nothing is 'lost'.
data.ActualFix: Effortless skills are read-only with respect to git after the one-time Step 0-6 bootstrap: only git status/diff/log are allowed. If the tree is dirty before a build, pause and ask the user for permission rather than committing/stashing for them; after a build, leave the dirty tree for the user to commit — never git add/commit/stash automatically.

data.Title: Writing a migration / ALTER TABLE on local-dev
data.LooksRight: Creating a migration file, a migrations tracking table, or running an incremental `ALTER TABLE` to make a schema change persist in the local-dev Postgres DB.
data.ActualFix: Local-dev ERB projects run `init-db.sh`, which drops and recreates the DB from scratch on every build — so the migration would run once and be wiped on the next build. The change only appears to stick until the next rebuild. The correct path is: edit the hub (effortless-rulebook.json) then run `effortless build`. (Bases-hosted DBs are the one exception, and schema still originates in the hub there too.)

data.Title: Reimplementing rule logic in the client
data.LooksRight: Computing `isStopped = customer.color === 'Red'` in JS instead of reading `customer.is_stopped` from the generated view.
data.ActualFix: The rule now lives in two places; when it changes in the hub (e.g. "now Green means stopped"), the client silently goes wrong because it wasn't rebuilt from the rulebook. Always consume calculated fields (e.g. `is_stopped`) from the view as opaque truth — never re-derive them client-side.

data.Title: Hand-editing generated files
data.LooksRight: Directly editing `postgres/01-05*.sql`, `dotnet/.../BaseClasses/*.cs`, or other generated output files to make a change.
data.ActualFix: Fine only as a throwaway hypothesis test — `effortless build` overwrites these files, so nothing persists. For real, persistent changes: edit the hub, or use the `*b-customize-*` files for things the hub genuinely can't model.

data.Title: Adding columns/fields directly in SQL or C#
data.LooksRight: Adding a new column or field straight into the generated SQL schema or generated C# model classes.
data.ActualFix: Same mechanic as hand-editing generated files — changes not originating in the hub don't survive the next `effortless build`. The field must be added to the hub so it regenerates correctly on every build.

data.Title: Reasoning from a stale build
data.LooksRight: Inspecting generated SQL/code on disk and drawing conclusions about current schema/behavior after the hub has since been changed.
data.ActualFix: If the hub changed since the last `effortless build`, the code on disk is out of date. Rebuild before drawing any conclusions from generated artifacts.

data.Title: "Just this once" editing of generated SQL
data.LooksRight: Skipping the build step and editing generated SQL directly, telling yourself it's a one-off exception.
data.ActualFix: There is no "just this once" — the next `effortless build` erases the edit and the bug returns. The very fact that the shortcut sounds reasonable is the tell that it's the wrong turn; always go around the loop (hub → build) instead.

data.Title: Treating an output spoke as if it were the source
data.LooksRight: Editing Postgres SQL, Go, Python, OWL, or XLSX output files directly, treating them as authoritative because they're the thing the app actually reads.
data.ActualFix: These are all *outputs* of the build. The single source of truth is `effortless-rulebook.json` (the hub). Edits to any output are ephemeral by design and will be overwritten on the next build.

data.Title: Editing installed skill copies instead of the SSoT clone
data.LooksRight: Directly editing a skill under ~/.claude/skills/effortless-* because that's the copy Claude Code actually loads and it's right there to tweak.
data.ActualFix: Never edit installed copies directly. Always edit in the SSoT clone (<clone>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md) and then run install.sh to propagate the change — the installed directory is downstream, not the source of truth.

data.Title: Auto-pulling/fetching git during an update-check
data.LooksRight: Running `git pull` or `git fetch` while just trying to check whether the local clone is behind upstream, since that seems like the natural way to 'check for updates'.
data.ActualFix: The check step is explicitly read-only: don't `git pull` or `git fetch` — just compare local HEAD to upstream via `gh api .../compare/$LOCAL...main` (or the curl/python3 fallback) without mutating the local repo. Actual pulling only happens in the separate 'Update: apply the latest' phase, and even there the skill notes 'ASK before running git commands' — the user authorizes each step.

data.Title: Summarizing behind-commits as 'minor'/'safe to skip'
data.LooksRight: When the compare shows `behind: N > 0`, glossing the commit list with a judgment call like 'these are just minor fixes, safe to skip' to save the user time.
data.ActualFix: List the commit messages as-is and let the user read and decide; don't summarize as 'minor' or 'safe to skip'.

data.Title: Installing CLI under the wrong Node version silently 'loses' it
data.LooksRight: Just running `npm install -g .` under whatever Node version happens to be the shell's current default at the time, without checking what Vite/the generated apps need.
data.ActualFix: Always install the CLI under the same Node version (18+, prefer 20+) that the user's generated apps will run on. If installed under an old Node and the user later `nvm use`s a different version, `which effortless` resolves to a different nvm prefix and the CLI appears to vanish. Also, `nvm alias default 20` only affects new shells — existing terminals keep the old version, so start.sh scripts must bake in an explicit Node-version check/switch.

data.Title: Downgrading Vite instead of fixing Node version
data.LooksRight: Seeing `crypto.getRandomValues is not a function` or ESM `node:` import errors from a generated Vite 5 app and concluding Vite itself is broken, so downgrading Vite to work around it.
data.ActualFix: This is a Node<18 symptom (Node 16 lacks `crypto.getRandomValues`), not a Vite bug. Check `node --version` first; the fix is upgrading/switching Node (and rebuilding `node_modules` that were built against Node 16: `rm -rf node_modules package-lock.json && npm install`), not downgrading Vite.

data.Title: Leaving stale legacy PKG symlinks to shadow the npm install
data.LooksRight: Running the npm install and assuming `effortless` now points at the new CLI, without checking PATH ordering — since the npm installer doesn't touch or remove old `/usr/local/bin/{ssotme,aicapture}` binaries from a legacy PKG installer.
data.ActualFix: Check `which -a effortless ssotme` and PATH order (`echo $PATH | tr ':' '\n' | grep -nE 'nvm|/usr/local/bin'`). If `/usr/local/bin` resolves first, the old legacy binary silently wins over the new npm-installed one; fix by reordering PATH or removing the legacy symlinks with explicit user confirmation.

data.Title: Wiring rulebook-to-airtable without disabling it
data.LooksRight: Installing `rulebook-to-airtable` (reverse-sync from rulebook back to Airtable) the same way as any other transpiler, leaving it enabled in `ProjectTranspilers`.
data.ActualFix: It MUST be installed with `IsDisabled: true` so a normal `effortless build` doesn't run it — only an explicit `effortless build -id` (include disabled) runs it. Otherwise every routine build would push rulebook state back into Airtable, potentially overwriting/conflicting with the intended one-way hub-first flow.

data.Title: Setting an Airtable API key for a Rulebook-First project
data.LooksRight: Assuming every Effortless project needs `-setAccountAPIKey airtable=...` configured up front as a standard setup step.
data.ActualFix: Rulebook-First projects (the default/best-practice) need no API key at all — API key management only applies to projects that have explicitly opted into Airtable as an input spoke. Also, every airtable-facing tool call must separately include `-account airtable` to actually inject the key; adding the key alone isn't sufficient.

data.Title: Using query_rulebook MCP tool instead of a local one-liner
data.LooksRight: Calling the `query_rulebook` MCP tool to inspect rulebook structure (tables/schema/relationships/etc.) since it's right there in the MCP surface and seems like the intended way to query a rulebook from an MCP-connected client.
data.ActualFix: When the CLI is available locally, use a local python one-liner (per the effortless-query skill) instead — `query_rulebook` adds a network round-trip for no benefit when local access exists.

data.Title: Using MCP transpiler tools for scalar Airtable field add/CRUD
data.LooksRight: Since MCP exposes ~54 transpiler tools including Airtable-related ones, it looks natural to route a scalar field add or CRUD operation through an MCP transpiler tool.
data.ActualFix: Scalar field add / CRUD should go through the Airtable REST API directly (see effortless-airtable), not the MCP transpiler tools.

data.Title: Using MCP/Airtable API for formula, lookup, rollup, or new-table changes
data.LooksRight: Attempting formula fields, lookup fields, rollup fields, or new table creation via the Airtable REST API (or an MCP tool) because that's the same surface used for scalar field changes.
data.ActualFix: These operations are not supported by the Airtable API and must go through OMNI via Playwright (see effortless-airtable-omni).

data.Title: Deploying a new MCP server version via cpln CLI directly
data.LooksRight: Running `cpln apply` / docker build/push manually to ship a new version of the MCP server, since that's the underlying mechanism.
data.ActualFix: Deploys must go through the transpiler-server UI at localhost:3000 (Publish New Version), which runs the build/push/apply AND inserts the required TranspilerVersion row in Airtable — a manual cpln apply would skip the Airtable record and version-bump steps (workload/ssotme-tool.json and package.json version bumps in bake-catalog.sh / bake-skills.sh sequence).

data.Title: Name field used as the lookup/match key instead of <Entity>Id
data.LooksRight: Writing an INDEX/MATCH lookup formula (or any FK resolution) that matches against a related table's `Name` field, e.g. MATCH({{Customer}}, Customers!{{Name}}, 0) — since Name is the human-readable label it seems like the natural thing to match on.
