data.ActualFix: Name is a calculated display alias, never the stored identity. The MATCH column must always be the related table's `<Entity>Id` raw field (e.g. Customers!{{CustomerId}}); FK fields hold the value of the parent's `<Entity>Id`, not its Name.

data.Title: FK field named with an 'Id' suffix like a traditional foreign key column
data.LooksRight: Naming a foreign key field `Order.CustomerId`, `Employee.RoleId`, or `Artifact.DerivedFromId` — mirroring conventional SQL FK-column naming (ColumnId referencing another table's PK).
data.ActualFix: ERB FK fields use the SINGULAR entity name with NO 'Id' suffix: `Order.Customer`, `Employee.Role`, `Artifact.DerivedFrom`. The 'Id' suffix is reserved for each table's own stored `<Entity>Id` identity field, not for FK fields pointing at other tables.

data.Title: Modeling a many-to-many relationship directly
data.LooksRight: Giving two tables a direct many-to-many relationship (e.g. Students <-> Courses) because that's how the real-world data relates and it's the familiar relational-modeling shortcut.
data.ActualFix: The rulebook is a DAG and many-to-many breaks the acyclic requirement. Always introduce a junction table with two 1-to-many relationships instead: Students -> Enrollments <- Courses, with Enrollment.Student and Enrollment.Course as singular FK fields.

data.Title: Materializing Name as a raw field to work around the old PK-collapse bug
data.LooksRight: Given the historical bug where a compound-Name PK could collapse onto just its first component (deduping distinct rows), it looks reasonable to 'fix' this by making Name a stored/raw field instead of calculated, so the PK synthesis has something stable to key off of.
data.ActualFix: This bug is already fixed in the published rulebook-to-postgres transpiler (full compound value is now used for PK synthesis, and an author-intended <Entity>Id still wins over incidental Id-suffixed attribute fields). No rulebook workaround is needed anymore — just rebuild with the published transpiler rather than materializing Name as raw.

data.Title: Storing magic-link/auth state in rulebook tables
data.LooksRight: Adding rulebook tables like `MagicLinkIntegration` or `ERBmagiclinks` to track auth/session state, since the rulebook is the SSoT for the app's data model so it seems like auth state belongs there too.
data.ActualFix: Auth state does not belong in the rulebook. The only source of truth is `auth.trusted_tenants` from install-magic-links.sql; offer migration away from any such rulebook tables when seen.

data.Title: v1 GUC-cache auth pattern instead of transaction-scoped auth.set_jwt
data.LooksRight: Node middleware calling raw `set_config('app.jwt_email', …)` directly and RLS policies reading `current_setting('app.jwt_email', true)` directly — looks like a simpler, more direct way to pass the authenticated identity into Postgres session config for RLS.
data.ActualFix: The correct v2 shape wraps every request in `BEGIN; SELECT auth.set_jwt($1); … COMMIT;` and RLS policies call the `app.jwt_email()` function rather than reading current_setting directly. Offer migration when the v1 pattern is seen.

data.Title: Reading generated SQL/Go/Python to understand the schema
data.LooksRight: Opening the generated SQL DDL, or Go/Python model files, to figure out table columns, types, or relationships — since those are the files the app actually runs against and look authoritative.
data.ActualFix: Those files are projections, not the source. The rulebook (effortless-rulebook.json, or its derived files) is the single source of schema truth — always query it instead.

data.Title: Loading the full rulebook JSON into context
data.LooksRight: Running `cat effortless-rulebook.json` or using the Read tool directly on the rulebook file 'to get a sense of things' or to answer a simple schema question.
data.ActualFix: The rulebook JSON can be megabytes (includes data rows). Use targeted python one-liner queries (or psql \d on the view) that extract only the needed table/field — 10-30 lines instead of thousands of tokens polluting context for the rest of the conversation.

data.Title: Jumping straight to the full rulebook when derived files exist
data.LooksRight: Ignoring the derived-* files (read-me-1st.txt, derived-schema.min.json, derived-schema.json) and going straight to running one-liner queries against, or reading, the full effortless-rulebook.json.
data.ActualFix: If minimize-rulebook is registered in effortless.json, climb the ladder from the top: read *.derived-read-me-1st.txt first (complete map in ~30 lines), then derived-schema.min.json, then derived-schema.json, and only fall back to the full effortless-rulebook.json if those don't answer the question.

data.Title: Reading derived-data.json just to browse
data.LooksRight: Opening *.derived-data.json to casually look at some example rows or 'get a sense' of the data while exploring the schema.
data.ActualFix: derived-data.json is the one file with actual data rows and should be read on demand only, when the task specifically requires seeing real row values — not for general browsing.

data.Title: Writing a migration/ALTER TABLE against local-dev Postgres
data.LooksRight: Hand-writing CREATE TABLE / ALTER TABLE / DROP TABLE / INSERT INTO against the local DB, adding a file under postgres/migrations/, or inserting into a migrations/schema_migrations tracking table on a local-dev project — these all look like normal, persistent schema changes.
data.ActualFix: Local-dev Postgres is dropped and recreated from scratch on every `effortless build` via init-db.sh, so none of these persist — they're silently wiped on the next build. The correct fix is to edit the hub (effortless-rulebook.json directly, or via Airtable if connected) and rerun `effortless build`. 'If the answer feels like write a migration, the answer is edit the rulebook.'

data.Title: Editing a generated 0*.sql file to fix schema/logic
data.LooksRight: Directly editing a generated file like 00-05*.sql to patch schema, a view, or a calculated field, since the change appears to take effect immediately.
data.ActualFix: Generated 0*.sql files are overwritten on the next build — the edit evaporates. Business schema/logic belongs in the hub (effortless-rulebook.json); only *b-customize-*.sql files (sized for infrastructure like auth tenants, JWT helpers, role GRANTs) survive rebuilds as hand-edited surfaces.

data.Title: Putting a new business entity in 01b-customize-schema.sql
data.LooksRight: Hand-writing 'CREATE TABLE app.foo (...)' inside 01b-customize-schema.sql for a new business table like Foo/Bar, since that file does survive the build (unlike generated files or raw migrations).
data.ActualFix: 01b-customize-* is sized for infrastructure (auth tenants, JWT helpers, role GRANTs), not business entities — business entities belong in the hub where they automatically get views (vw_*) and calculated fields for free. Edit effortless-rulebook.json (or Airtable) instead, then `effortless build`.

data.Title: Treating a Bases-hosted DB the same as local-dev (or vice versa)
data.LooksRight: Assuming all Postgres targets either always use migrations or never do — e.g. writing a raw migration against a Bases-hosted DB expecting it to be 'wiped like local-dev', or dropping/recreating a Bases-hosted DB the way local-dev is handled.
data.ActualFix: bases.effortlessapi.com-hosted databases can't be dropped + recreated, so they DO use migrations — but applied via postgres/apply-migration.sh, not raw psql, and the migration is still a delivery mechanism for a hub delta (schema still originates in the hub), not a place to author schema from scratch. Check for BASES_DATABASE_URL in .env.example or a 'Bases is migration-only' block in CLAUDE.md before touching Postgres to know which regime applies.

data.Title: Silently rerouting to a different input spoke when one is blocked
data.LooksRight: When the Airtable API can't create a formula field (or there's no API key, or the project isn't Airtable-connected), quietly falling back to editing a generated file or another surface to 'get the change in' so the task appears done.
data.ActualFix: Pause and surface the blocker instead of silently switching — edits to generated files are ephemeral anyway, so the apparent fix would evaporate on the next build. Lay out the real alternatives (rulebook-direct, Airtable UI, reverse-sync, customization files) and wait for the user's direction.

data.Title: Rebuilding or editing the hub without asking, or auto-committing after a build
data.LooksRight: Proactively editing effortless-rulebook.json, running `effortless build`, or running an individual transpiler because it's clearly the 'correct' next step — then committing the resulting diff to keep things tidy, since the build succeeded.
data.ActualFix: These operations change the hub and cascade through every output spoke, so the developer must choose when that cascade fires — always ask permission first. Also check `git status --porcelain` before building (read-only) and flag non-obvious pending changes; after the build, never auto-commit — leave the dirty tree for the user to commit (except the one authorized exception: effortless-setup-postgres's initial bootstrap commits).

data.Title: Reading generated files/SQL to "verify" a build
data.LooksRight: After running `effortless build`, cat the generated SQL files, read the output files, or load skills to interpret build output to make sure the build "worked" or to understand what changed.
data.ActualFix: `effortless build` is atomic and deterministic — same rulebook in, same artifact out. Treat it like `npm install`: run it and trust it worked. Do NOT read generated files afterward; if you need schema info post-build, query the rulebook directly (effortless-query) or `psql -c "\d vw_tablename"` instead of reading generated SQL.

data.Title: Committing on the user's behalf after a build
data.LooksRight: After `effortless build` leaves the working tree dirty with regenerated files, run `git add`/`git commit` to tidy up or finish the task.
data.ActualFix: Never commit on the user's behalf. Leave the dirty tree for the user to commit when they choose. Effortless skills only ever read git (status/diff/log); they never drive it (add/commit/etc).

data.Title: Authoring business entities/schema directly in a migration file
data.LooksRight: On a Bases-connected project (or any project with a `migrations/` folder), add or edit a migration file directly to introduce a new business entity or schema change, since that's where the SQL deltas live.
data.ActualFix: Schema always originates in the rulebook, even on the Bases deployment shape. Bases migrations only *deliver* rulebook-derived deltas to a DB that can't be dropped — never author business entities directly in a migration file.

data.Title: Writing a migration on a local-dev Postgres project
data.LooksRight: Since Postgres migrations exist as a concept in the pipeline, write/apply a migration file on a plain local-dev project to make a schema change.
data.ActualFix: Local-dev Postgres has no `migrations/` folder and no tracking table — `init-db.sh` simply drops and recreates the DB on every build. If the project has no `BASES_DATABASE_URL` and no "Bases is migration-only" block in CLAUDE.md, it's local-dev: no migrations, ever. (Migrations only apply on the Bases deployment shape.)

data.Title: Running the reverse-sync (rulebook-to-airtable) tool during a normal build
data.LooksRight: Leave `rulebook-to-airtable` enabled in `push-to-airtable/effortless.json` so a normal `effortless build` keeps Airtable automatically in sync with the rulebook.
data.ActualFix: `rulebook-to-airtable` MUST be installed with `"IsDisabled": true` so normal `effortless build` skips it. It is only invoked explicitly via `effortless build -id` from the `push-to-airtable/` directory for intentional reverse-sync.

data.Title: Running reverse-sync with drop/overwrite semantics against a shared base
data.LooksRight: Use the nuclear/drop-all rebuild mode against any Airtable/Postgres base by default since it's simpler and guarantees a clean state.
data.ActualFix: Always run with `check-don't-drop` (check-add mode) against any base you didn't create in the same conversation — it's safe and preserves data. Nuclear/drop-all is localhost-only, refused by the transpiler for staging/prod, and only opt-in when the user explicitly types it.

data.Title: Editing Airtable directly when it's only a downstream mirror
data.LooksRight: Editing fields/records in the Airtable UI or API for a project where Airtable is wired as an output spoke only (rulebook-to-airtable, no airtable-to-rulebook input), assuming those edits will persist or feed back into the hub.
data.ActualFix: If the project is not Airtable-connected as an input spoke (baseId missing or airtable-to-rulebook disabled), edit effortless-rulebook.json directly instead — Airtable in that direction is an output, and `effortless build` will overwrite any direct Airtable edits with whatever the hub says.

data.Title: Editing generated/downstream files to work around an Airtable API limitation
data.LooksRight: When the Airtable API can't create/modify a formula field (or other unsupported operation), silently switching to hand-editing the generated output files to make it 'work'.
data.ActualFix: Don't silently switch to editing generated files — those edits get overwritten on the next build, so the apparent fix would evaporate. Instead surface the blocker and let the user choose: rulebook-direct edit (+ reverse-sync if Airtable-connected), OMNI via Playwright, manual Airtable UI edit, or a customization file for non-modelable SQL.

data.Title: Assuming formula fields can be created/modified via the Airtable API
data.LooksRight: Calling the standard field-create/PATCH endpoints with type 'formula' expecting it to work like other field types (singleLineText, checkbox, etc.).
data.ActualFix: Formula fields (and by extension lookup/rollup) cannot be created or modified via the Airtable API at all — this requires a different path (effortless-airtable-omni via Playwright, or rulebook-direct + reverse-sync).

data.Title: Searching the filesystem/config for the Airtable API key before checking the env var
data.LooksRight: Grepping config files or searching the filesystem for the Airtable API key first, or reading ~/.ssotme/ssotme.key / effortless.json before checking the environment.
data.ActualFix: Always check `$AIRTABLE_API_KEY` first; only fall back to ~/.ssotme/ssotme.key then effortless.json's ProjectSettings._apikey_ if the env var is empty.

data.Title: Modifying Airtable/rulebook without asking the user first
data.LooksRight: Going ahead and making the schema/data change (in either direction) as soon as a plausible fix is identified.
data.ActualFix: In either direction (Airtable-spoke or reverse-sync), always ask the user for permission before modifying the rulebook or Airtable.

data.Title: Using OMNI for scalar field changes or CRUD
data.LooksRight: Reaching for OMNI (the Playwright/AI-driven browser tool) to add any field or make any Airtable change, since it 'can do anything' via natural-language prompts.
data.ActualFix: OMNI is an escape hatch, not the default. Scalar field changes (text, number, checkbox, select, date, url, linked records/FKs), all CRUD, field renaming/descriptions must go through the Airtable REST API directly (effortless-airtable skill). OMNI is reserved ONLY for what the API truly cannot do: formula fields, lookup fields, rollup fields, and new-table creation (which needs the Name formula).

data.Title: Believing the API can create the Name formula field
data.LooksRight: Trying to create a new ERB table's required `Name` field (e.g. `SUBSTITUTE(LOWER({DisplayName}), " ", "-")`) via the Airtable API's POST /fields endpoint since it's 'just a field'.
data.ActualFix: Formula field creation is unsupported by the API entirely — the Name formula (and any formula field) can only be created via OMNI. This is also why creating a brand-new table always requires OMNI, even though table creation itself might seem like an API-doable action.

data.Title: Including {Entity}Id surrogate-key fields in OMNI prompts
data.LooksRight: Explicitly telling OMNI to add an `{Entity}Id` field when defining a new table's fields, since it seems like the primary key should be spelled out.
data.ActualFix: NEVER include `{Entity}Id` fields in OMNI prompts — surrogate keys are managed off-screen (auto-generated), not created via OMNI schema prompts.

data.Title: Telling OMNI to create a 'boolean' field
data.LooksRight: Prompting OMNI with 'Add a boolean field called IsActive' since that's the semantic type being modeled.
data.ActualFix: Airtable's native type for booleans is Checkbox, not boolean. OMNI prompts must always say 'Checkbox field' (e.g. 'Add a Checkbox field called "IsActive"') or the field type may not resolve correctly.

data.Title: Batching multiple computed-field requests into one OMNI prompt
data.LooksRight: Sending one large prompt describing several formulas/lookups at once to save round-trips.
data.ActualFix: Send one computed field at a time — this is documented as more reliable than batching; the granular strategy is to request, verify via stdout, kill the browser, then repeat for the next field.

data.Title: Skipping `effortless build` after an OMNI schema change
data.LooksRight: Finishing an OMNI operation (e.g. adding a lookup or formula field) and moving on without rebuilding, since the Airtable base itself is already updated.
data.ActualFix: Always run `effortless build` after Airtable changes made via OMNI so the Airtable spoke is pulled into the rulebook hub and downstream output spokes regenerate — except mid-batch during a reverse-sync mirroring session, where you wait until all changes are done and build once at the end.

data.Title: Using standard SQL-ish formula syntax in OMNI prompts
data.LooksRight: Writing Airtable formulas with `<>` for not-equal, `ISBLANK()` for blank checks, or prefixing formulas with `=` as one would in Excel/SQL.
data.ActualFix: Airtable formula syntax differs: not-equal is `!=` (not `<>`), blank check is `{Field} = BLANK()` (not `ISBLANK()`), and formulas do NOT start with `=`.

data.Title: Reading from base tables instead of vw_* views
data.LooksRight: SELECT * FROM customers WHERE hair_color = 'red'; — querying the base table directly since it 'has the data you need'
data.ActualFix: Always SELECT from the vw_<table> view instead: SELECT * FROM vw_customers WHERE is_red_headed = true; — views include raw fields plus every calculated/lookup/aggregation field computed via generated SQL functions. Base tables only have raw columns, and recomputing the logic yourself (e.g. LOWER(hair_color)='red') duplicates business logic that already lives in the rulebook and risks inconsistency.

data.Title: JOINing two vw_* views to pull a related entity's field
data.LooksRight: SELECT m.mail_item_id, w.last_name AS ward_last_name FROM vw_mail_items m JOIN vw_wards w ON w.ward_id = m.ward WHERE m.mail_item_id = $1; — looks fine because both sides are 'proper' views, not base tables
data.ActualFix: Add a lookup field to the rulebook (e.g. MailItems.WardLastName via INDEX/MATCH formula), rebuild, then read a single view: SELECT mail_item_id, ward_last_name FROM vw_mail_items WHERE mail_item_id = $1. A JOIN across views means the rulebook is missing a lookup field — the relationship belongs in the rulebook DAG, not app SQL, so every consumer gets the column for free without repeating the JOIN.

data.Title: Editing generated SQL files (00-05) directly
data.LooksRight: Hand-editing postgres/01-drop-and-create-tables.sql, 02-create-functions.sql, 03-create-views.sql, etc. to add a column, fix a function, or tweak a view — the change appears to work immediately
data.ActualFix: These files are mechanical output of the rulebook hub, rewritten on every `effortless build`; any manual edit is silently lost on the next build. To make a change stick, edit the hub (effortless-rulebook.json / Airtable). If the hub genuinely can't express the need, use the corresponding *b-customize-*.sql file (01b/02b/03b/04b/05b), which runs after the generated file and is preserved across builds.

data.Title: Treating local-dev Postgres as a migrated database
data.LooksRight: Creating a migrations/ folder or a migrations-tracking table, or writing an incremental ALTER TABLE delta script for the local-dev DB
data.ActualFix: init-db.sh drops and recreates the local DB on every build, so any migration-tracking artifact gets wiped on the next build. Schema changes belong in the hub, followed by `effortless build`. The only place deltas are the real mechanism is a bases.effortlessapi.com-hosted DB (via postgres/apply-migration.sh) where the DB can't be dropped — but even then the schema still originates in the hub.

data.Title: Adding a business-entity table via a *b-customize-* file
data.LooksRight: Reaching for 01b-customize-schema.sql to CREATE TABLE a new business entity like `Foo` because it's 'preserved across builds' and easy to add to
data.ActualFix: *b-customize-* files are meant for idempotent infrastructure the hub doesn't model (auth tenants, JWT helpers, role GRANTs) — they re-run on every fresh init-db.sh, so they must stay idempotent, not one-shot. For business entities like `Foo`, the table belongs in the rulebook itself so it participates in the calculated-field DAG, views, and RLS generation.

data.Title: Wrong JWT source for talking to bases
data.LooksRight: Using the magic-links self-auth flow (POST {MAGICLINK}/auth/send-code → /auth/verify-code) to get a JWT and then calling bases.effortlessapi.com or bases-api.effortlessapi.com with it — this looks right because magic-links is the general-purpose auth server and older documentation described this flow.
data.ActualFix: Bases does not trust the magic-links tenant. Use the bases-api-specific auth flow instead: POST {BASES_API}/auth/email-auth then POST {BASES_API}/auth/magic-link to get a JWT bases actually accepts. The magic-links self-auth JWTs have a different `iss` and get rejected by bases as "Unknown tenant".

data.Title: Listing bases from the Node service instead of the .NET service
data.LooksRight: Calling `GET {BASES}/bases` (the Node dashboard server) to enumerate a user's bases, since Node is the service you register/clone bases through.
data.ActualFix: Node's underlying view is stale/older and doesn't surface .NET-created bases. Use `GET {BASES_API}/api/bases` (the .NET CRUD service) as the authoritative list/read source; use Node only to create, clone, apply privileges, and manage auth.

data.Title: Assuming source:"empty" bases are unsupported / cloning a template unnecessarily
data.LooksRight: Believing you must always clone an existing base (via `sourceBaseId`) or supply a real Airtable PAT+baseId to provision a new base, because older notes said `source:"empty"` was local-only / undeployed.
data.ActualFix: `{"source":"empty",...}` is deployed (as of Jul 2026) and provisions a blank base directly — no PAT, no Airtable base id, no need to clone a template.

data.Title: Expecting GET /auth/credentials to work immediately after base creation
data.LooksRight: Calling `GET {BASES}/bases/{baseId}/auth/credentials` right after creating a base to fetch Postgres role passwords.
data.ActualFix: That endpoint 404s until the privilege template has been applied at least once. Call `POST {BASES}/bases/{baseId}/auth/apply-privileges-template` with `returnCredentials:true` first — that both creates the roles and returns the passwords on the first call.

data.Title: Installing JWT helper functions as app-side SQL / via the base admin role
data.LooksRight: Hand-fetching `install.sql` and running it yourself (or writing your own plpython3u RS256 verifier + `auth.set_jwt`/`app.jwt_*` helpers) as the base's `<db>_admin` role, since that's how other schema/SQL changes are applied.
data.ActualFix: The base ADMIN role cannot `CREATE EXTENSION` (needed for plpython3u/PyJWT); only the operator superuser can install these helpers, and that only happens by calling `POST {BASES}/bases/{baseId}/auth/setup-trusted-tenants`. The helper install must go through that endpoint, not app-side psql.

data.Title: Believing a PAT / Airtable integration or an AppUsers table is required for basic RLS
data.LooksRight: Refusing to set up magic-links RLS on a base until a PAT/Airtable integration and an AppUsers table (userTableName/emailField/roleField/isActiveField) are configured, because the endpoint used to hard-fail with "PAT not configured for this base".
data.ActualFix: That gate was removed (Jul 2026 fix). PAT/Airtable upsert now only runs if a PAT already exists; basic per-email RLS via `setup-trusted-tenants` needs neither a PAT nor an AppUsers table — that table is only needed for Tier-2 role-based RLS.

data.Title: Running effortless build / init-db.sh against a bases database
data.LooksRight: Running the normal local-dev rebuild flow (`effortless build`, which regenerates via `init-db.sh`) against a bases-hosted database when you want to apply schema changes — this is the standard ERB way to apply schema everywhere else.
data.ActualFix: Bases is the one deployment shape that uses migrations because the DB is shared/persistent and can't be dropped and recreated. The generated `init-db.sh` greps for `bases.effortlessapi.com` in `$DATABASE_URL` and refuses with exit 2 (no escape hatch). After the first schema apply, all further changes go through hand-written idempotent migrations under `postgres/migrations/NNNN-*.sql` applied via `postgres/apply-migration.sh`.

data.Title: Editing 04b-customize-policies.sql and rebuilding to change RLS on bases
data.LooksRight: Modifying the generated `04b-customize-policies.sql` customize file and rebuilding to add/change an RLS policy on a bases base, since that's the normal customize-file pattern for schema/function/view customizations elsewhere.
data.ActualFix: That file gets dropped/overwritten on the next rebuild. RLS policy changes for bases must live in migration files (via `apply-migration.sh`), not in the customize-file + rebuild pattern.

data.Title: Trusting a stale HEAD-vs-deployed assumption about bases.effortlessapi.com behavior
data.LooksRight: Assuming a feature described in the skill (or recently changed in `src/routes/bases.js`) is live in production because it's merged to `origin/main` or present in the skill text.
data.ActualFix: There is an observed deploy lag (e.g. `source:"empty"` was in HEAD before it was in production). Check `git log -1 origin/main` against actually-deployed behavior before claiming a feature is live, and if you change the route source, update both the deployed service and this skill in the same PR.

data.Title: Reusing one magic-links tenant across unrelated apps, or minting a second tenant for a downstream consumer
data.LooksRight: Either (a) sharing a single magic-links tenant across multiple unrelated products for convenience, or (b) minting a brand-new tenant for a downstream consumer app that shares a base, since each app/service normally gets its own auth setup.
data.ActualFix: One tenant per product surface (don't reuse across unrelated apps) — but for a downstream app that's part of the same product/topology, share the existing tenant's public key by inserting the same `(tenant_id, public_key_pem)` row into the downstream DB's `auth.trusted_tenants`, rather than minting a second tenant.

data.Title: Setting JWT claims from application code instead of via auth.set_jwt
data.LooksRight: Using `set_config(...)` or `SET LOCAL app.jwt_*` directly from app code to make jwt claims available to RLS policies.
data.ActualFix: Never do this — the downstream/consumer middleware should open a transaction and call `SELECT auth.set_jwt($1)` with the raw token; RLS then reads `app.jwt_email()`/`app.has_role()` from that.

data.Title: Connecting to bases Postgres with sslmode=require
data.LooksRight: Appending `sslmode=require` to the bases Postgres connection string, as is standard practice for hosted Postgres, or setting `ssl: true` in a Node pg client.
data.ActualFix: The bases Postgres on :5432 does not currently terminate TLS; `sslmode=require` causes psql to fail with "server does not support SSL, but SSL was required". Connect without it (`ssl: false` in Node/pg), and re-verify this before changing the assumption since it's an empirically-observed, possibly-temporary fact rather than a permanent guarantee.

data.Title: Hand-rolling an AppUsers/Profiles table under app.* / auth.*
data.LooksRight: Creating app.app_users, app.users, or app.profiles by hand in 01b-customize-schema.sql because that's where auth-adjacent SQL lives
data.ActualFix: AppUsers is a rulebook entity (regenerated as public.app_users + vw_app_users) in the consuming app's ERB project. The only legitimate hand-written tables in auth/app are auth.trusted_tenants and the app.jwt_*() helper functions. A hand-mirrored users table drifts from the rulebook, never appears in views, and collides once someone adds it correctly.

data.Title: Looking up auth.trusted_tenants by iss instead of tenant_id
data.LooksRight: Keying the JWT verifier's tenant registry lookup off the iss claim, since iss visually looks like a tenant identifier (it's the full magiclink URL + tenant id)
data.ActualFix: The registry's primary key is the bare UUID (tenant_id claim), not the URL-shaped iss. Look up by tenant_id, then separately pass the decoded iss to the JWT library as the expected issuer. Confusing the two means the registry lookup silently misses every token.

data.Title: Forgetting to pass issuer when verifying the JWT
data.LooksRight: Verifying the JWT's signature and expiry with jwt.verify() but omitting the issuer option, since the token 'checks out' cryptographically
data.ActualFix: Without an explicit issuer check, a JWT minted for ANY tenant hosted by the same magic-links instance would pass verification — a cross-tenant auth bug. Pass the decoded iss (the full URL form, not the bare tenant UUID) as the expected issuer.

data.Title: v1 GUC-cache pattern: app code sets app.jwt_email directly
data.LooksRight: Middleware decodes/verifies the JWT in app code, then calls set_config('app.jwt_email', email, true) so RLS policies can read current_setting('app.jwt_email', true)
data.ActualFix: This is the deprecated v1 anti-pattern — RLS still fires, but the database trusts whatever the app wrote without verifying it itself. Correct v2 shape: hand the raw bearer token to SELECT auth.set_jwt($1) inside a transaction; the helper RS256-verifies against auth.trusted_tenants and populates transaction-local GUCs itself. RLS policies must call app.jwt_email() / app.jwt_tenant_id() / app.has_role(), never current_setting(...) directly.

data.Title: Testing RLS/GUCs without wrapping in BEGIN/COMMIT
data.LooksRight: Running SELECT auth.set_jwt(token); SELECT app.jwt_email(); as separate statements/psql invocations to smoke-test
data.ActualFix: The GUCs set by auth.set_jwt are transaction-local (by design, so a pooled connection can't leak identity to the next request). Outside a BEGIN/COMMIT block they evaporate between statements and the test reads NULL. Always wrap the smoke test in BEGIN ... COMMIT.

data.Title: Hand-decoding a JWT instead of verifying its signature
data.LooksRight: Using atob(jwt.split('.')[1]) (or equivalent base64-decode) to read claims and treating that as sufficient auth
data.ActualFix: That only decodes the payload — it does not verify the signature. Always RS256-verify against the saved public_key_pem before trusting any claim. Decoding without verifying is a debug tool, not auth.

data.Title: Trusting send-code's ok:true as proof the tenant exists
data.LooksRight: Treating a 200 {ok:true} from POST /api/tenants/{id}/send-code as confirmation the wiring/tenant is correct during first-time setup or smoke testing
data.ActualFix: Upstream send-code always returns ok:true even for a non-existent tenant. Always pair first wire-up verification with GET /api/tenants/{id} to confirm the tenant actually exists before trusting the send-code response.

data.Title: Trying to set an infinite / exp-less JWT for 'never sign in again'
data.LooksRight: Looking for a way to mint a token with no exp claim to give truly permanent sessions
data.ActualFix: There is deliberately no infinite/claim-less token — every base's Postgres verifier installs with verify_exp:True and hard-requires exp, so an exp-less token fails every RLS query. jwt_expires_in_seconds is clamped to [60s, 10 years]; the longest practical option is a large finite lifetime like 365 days (31536000), set via PATCH.

data.Title: Lengthening the wrong tenant's token lifetime for a bases app
data.LooksRight: PATCHing jwt_expires_in_seconds on the app's own magic-links tenant to extend session length for a bases-backed app
data.ActualFix: For a base's own auth (app talking to bases.effortlessapi.com), the JWT is minted by the bases magic-links tenant, not the app's tenant — jwt_expires_in_seconds must be set on that bases tenant, not the app's end-user tenant.

data.Title: Storing tenant_id / public_key_pem in the rulebook, or modeling auth as rulebook tables
data.LooksRight: Adding TENANT_ID/public key fields to the rulebook, or creating an ERBmagiclinks / MagicLinkIntegration entity so auth config is versioned like other domain data
data.ActualFix: Never put tenant_id / public_key_pem in the rulebook, and never create ERBmagiclinks or MagicLinkIntegration tables. Auth configuration lives only in auth.trusted_tenants (and env vars for the app-side tenant config) — it is explicitly out-of-band from the rulebook.

data.Title: Confusing the token field name between self-auth and tenant verify-code
data.LooksRight: Reading the JWT off the response as .jwt after calling /auth/verify-code (the self-auth endpoint), by analogy with /api/tenants/{id}/verify-code
data.ActualFix: /auth/verify-code (self-auth) returns {token, expires_in, user} — the field is token. /api/tenants/{id}/verify-code (end-user login) returns the JWT under jwt. Using the wrong field name silently yields undefined.

data.Title: Patching app code to recompute a missing field instead of extending the hub
data.LooksRight: A JOIN is fetching a field the view doesn't expose, so it seems reasonable to just add the extra JOIN back (or compute the value in application code) to get the data you need right now.
data.ActualFix: Extend the hub (rulebook-direct or via Airtable) so the field shows up in the view on the next build; patching the app to recompute it duplicates the rule instead of fixing the source of truth.

data.Title: Reading from base tables / hand-written JOINs instead of generated views
data.LooksRight: Querying base tables directly with JOINs (e.g. `FROM bids b JOIN companies c ON ... JOIN rfps r ON ...`) to assemble the data a screen needs, since the base tables clearly contain the columns.
data.ActualFix: Select from the generated `vw_*` view directly (e.g. `FROM vw_bids WHERE bid_id = $1`) — JOINs in application code are an anti-pattern; base tables should mostly only be touched for INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, with reads going through views.

data.Title: Hand-written JOIN in app code instead of a lookup field
data.LooksRight: SELECT a.*, b.foo FROM a JOIN b ON ... written directly in application code to get related data
data.ActualFix: Add a lookup field on table a pointing through the FK to b.foo, and read from the generated vw_* view instead of hand-joining

data.Title: Summing/aggregating in app code instead of a rollup field
data.LooksRight: total = sum(line.amount for line in order.lines) computed in application code
data.ActualFix: Add a rollup field like Order.TotalAmount to the rulebook and consume it as opaque truth rather than recomputing

data.Title: Recomputed derived boolean logic scattered across call sites
data.LooksRight: if user.is_admin and order.status == 'open': ... re-implemented in multiple places in app code
data.ActualFix: Add a calculated Is{Something} boolean field on the rulebook and reference it everywhere, so the logic can't drift between call sites

data.Title: Overwriting a row in place instead of bitemporal insert
data.LooksRight: UPDATE customers SET email = ? WHERE id = ? — overwriting the existing row
data.ActualFix: Insert a new fact with valid-time bounds and let the substrate retain history, since destroying prior state breaks the bitemporal 'what did we believe and when' guarantee

data.Title: Raw many-to-many junction table instead of a first-class entity
data.LooksRight: Adding a raw join table like student_courses directly without a corresponding model entity
data.ActualFix: Promote the junction to a first-class entity (e.g. Enrollment) with two 1-to-many FKs, since many-to-many breaks the DAG's acyclicity requirement

data.Title: Editing generated SQL/code/docs to 'fix a bug'
data.LooksRight: Editing postgres/00-05*.sql or generated Python/Go/docs directly because it looks like the fastest way to patch a bug
data.ActualFix: Trace back to the rulebook entry that produced the artifact, fix the rule there, and rebuild — the build will correctly erase any direct edit to the generated projection

data.Title: Adding a field directly to a generated Postgres view
data.LooksRight: ALTER VIEW or otherwise adding a column straight onto a generated vw_* view in Postgres
data.ActualFix: Add the field to the rulebook itself (or to a *b-customize-* seam if the rulebook genuinely cannot express it), since the view is generated from the rulebook and is not the SSoT

data.Title: Hand-written ORM model restating the schema
data.LooksRight: Writing an ORM class/type in Python or TypeScript that manually restates the table's fields and types
data.ActualFix: Generate the language binding from the rulebook via an existing transpiler instead of hand-authoring a parallel schema definition, to avoid re-fragmenting the single source of truth

data.Title: {Entity}Id surrogate columns appearing in the rulebook
data.LooksRight: Adding an {Entity}Id column directly into the rulebook, treating it like the logical primary key
data.ActualFix: Use Name (the kebab-cased compound formula) as the logical PK in the rulebook; surrogate IDs are minted off-screen by the substrate, not modeled in the rulebook

data.Title: Manually-updated cached calculated column
data.LooksRight: A calculated value stored in a column that the application code updates/writes to manually whenever inputs change
data.ActualFix: Replace the manually-maintained cached column with a formula field so the substrate recomputes it deterministically on read, preserving F + ACID guarantees

data.Title: New small admin/lookup/auth table created directly in Postgres
data.LooksRight: Creating a new 'auth users' or small lookup/admin table directly in Postgres because it seems minor or infrastructural rather than a 'real' business entity
data.ActualFix: Add the table to effortless-rulebook.json (or via Airtable if that input spoke is enabled) and rebuild — the rulebook is where all business entities live, with no exceptions for 'small' tables

data.Title: Triggers/stored procedures hiding business rules in Postgres
data.LooksRight: Implementing business logic as a Postgres trigger or stored procedure so it runs automatically at the DB layer
data.ActualFix: Move the logic into the rulebook as a formula or aggregation so every substrate (not just Postgres) can render/project it, preserving substrate equivalence

data.Title: 'TODO: keep this in sync with X' comment
data.LooksRight: Leaving a comment like 'TODO: keep this in sync with X' as an acceptable way to manage two places that must agree
data.ActualFix: Treat the comment itself as the diagnostic signal of drift risk — find the rulebook entry that should generate both instead of manually synchronizing them

data.Title: ORMs re-fragment the SSoT via hand-written JOINs and restated schema
data.LooksRight: Using an ORM: restate the schema as model classes in application code, write business-rule logic as application methods, and hand-write JOINs to combine related data — this looks like normal, idiomatic backend development.
data.ActualFix: Don't restate the schema or recompute derived values in app code. Declare lookups/aggregations/formulas in the rulebook and read from the generated `vw_*` views that already materialize them; application code treats the view's derived values as opaque truth and never recomputes them. (Skill points to `effortless-diagnostics` for the JOIN-in-app-code anti-pattern and `effortless-sql` for the views-vs-tables discipline.)

data.Title: Loading the skeptic-register skill for a friendly exploratory question
data.LooksRight: Any evaluative or 'why' question about ERB (e.g. 'is this any good', 'could this work for X') gets answered by loading effortless-rationale and mounting a receipts-based defense.
data.ActualFix: effortless-rationale is only for openly skeptical / adversarial conversations. Friendly-but-exploratory evaluative questions should instead be answered from inside the conjecture using effortless-orchestrator's Evaluative Posture plus effortless-cmcc — loading the rationale skill in that case turns a collaborative moment into an unwanted debate.

data.Title: Using ExcelJS / npm xlsx libraries instead of the transpiler
data.LooksRight: Installing ExcelJS (or another npm xlsx-writing package) and writing in-process JS code to build the workbook from query results, since that's the standard Node.js way to generate Excel files.
data.ActualFix: Use the `effortless rulebook-to-xlsx` transpiler, which reads a populated `rulebook-export.json` and produces the workbook. No npm dependency, no in-process spreadsheet logic — this keeps export generation consistent with the rulebook-driven pipeline instead of duplicating formatting/column logic in application code.

data.Title: Using execSync to invoke the transpiler
data.LooksRight: Calling the `effortless rulebook-to-xlsx` CLI synchronously via `execSync` since it's simpler to write than managing a child process with `spawn`.
data.ActualFix: Always use `spawn` (async) to invoke the transpiler — `execSync` blocks the Node event loop, which stalls the whole server (including unrelated requests) while the export runs.

data.Title: Querying base tables instead of vw_* views for export data
data.LooksRight: Populating the rulebook-export.json data arrays by querying the raw Postgres base tables directly, since that seems like the straightforward way to get 'the data'.
data.ActualFix: Query each `vw_*` view instead — because calculated, lookup, and aggregation columns only exist on the views, reading from base tables silently drops all derived columns from the export. Reading views is also the general ERB convention, not specific to this skill's warning, but the skill explicitly ties correctness of the export ('calculated fields are automatic') to reading from vw_* views.

data.Title: Hand-writing effortless.json
data.LooksRight: Creating or editing effortless.json directly to add a transpiler or fix a config value.
data.ActualFix: effortless.json is generated by `effortless -init` and owned/maintained by the CLI. Never write or edit it directly — use `effortless -install <transpiler>` to add transpilers instead.

data.Title: Manually running init-db.sh when the DB doesn't update
data.LooksRight: If the DB doesn't reflect schema changes after `effortless build`, running `init-db.sh` manually to force it.
data.ActualFix: The real problem is the init-db exec tool wasn't installed in the scaffold step; fix that registration (RelativePath `/postgres`, CommandLine `-exec init-db.sh`) so `effortless build` runs it automatically — don't manually invoke init-db.sh as a workaround.

data.Title: Leaving generated init-db.sh pointed at the generic 'demo' DB
data.LooksRight: Running `effortless build` and using the generated postgres/init-db.sh as-is, since it already has a DEFAULT_CONN and header comment.
data.ActualFix: The transpiler's default (`DEFAULT_CONN=postgresql://postgres@localhost:5432/demo`, header `# demo - Database Initialization Script`) is a generic placeholder that is wrong once it's a named project. Anyone running `./init-db.sh` without DATABASE_URL set will silently hit the unrelated `demo` DB. This skill's job is to patch DEFAULT_CONN and the header comment to the project's actual DB name immediately after every build (re-apply if the transpiler stomps it back) — do not file it as a transpiler bug.

data.Title: Lookups/FKs keyed on Name instead of <Entity>Id
data.LooksRight: Writing a MATCH/lookup formula against the related table's `Name` field, or storing a `Name` value in an FK column, since Name looks like the natural identifier.
data.ActualFix: `Name` is always a calculated display alias, never the stored PK and never used in lookups. FK columns must hold the value of the related table's `<Entity>Id`, and MATCH must always target `<Entity>Id` — never `Name`.

data.Title: Patching broken lookups with a LEFT JOIN in customize-views or a cross-table subquery in app code
data.LooksRight: When a lookup 'isn't resolving' or a page needs data scoped by a related table, adding a `LEFT JOIN` in `03b-customize-views.sql`, or writing `WHERE x IN (SELECT y FROM other_view)` in app code to scope results.
data.ActualFix: If a lookup isn't resolving, the bug is almost always in the rulebook FK pattern (FK column holding a Name value instead of an <Entity>Id value) — fix the rulebook, don't paper over it with a JOIN. `vw_*` views must stay join-free; customize files are only for additive views/columns/functions, not an escape hatch. For app-code filtering, add a (possibly chained) lookup column to the rulebook and filter on that instead of a cross-table subquery.

data.Title: Trusting declared datatype for time-like field names
data.LooksRight: Declaring `datatype: "string"` for a free-text field named with a token like `*Time`, `*Date`, `*Period`, `*HHMM`, or `*_at` and assuming the generated SQL column will actually be text.
data.ActualFix: Field-name inference can override the declared datatype — such names may get coerced to DATE/TIMESTAMPTZ regardless of what you wrote. Use a neutral name instead (e.g. `ClockLabel`, `BillingTag`) if you need genuinely free-text content.

data.Title: Assuming base tables have a 'name' column / writing to it
data.LooksRight: Trying to INSERT/UPDATE a `name` column on a base table, or assuming the PK column is literally named `id` or `name`.
data.ActualFix: Name is calculated only in the view, re-derived from its formula on every read; base tables don't have a name column. The PK column on the base table is `<table>_id`; application writes (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) must target `<table>_id` and only touch raw columns — reads go through the view.

data.Title: Calculated PK/Name formulas concatenating a coerced date/timestamp field
data.LooksRight: Building `Name = CONCAT(...)` where one of the concatenated fields got coerced to DATE/TIMESTAMPTZ by field-name inference, expecting the resulting string to match string FK values used elsewhere.
data.ActualFix: CONCAT on a timestamp emits something like `2026-05-01 00:00:00-05`, not `2026-05-01`, so the composed Name won't match stored FK slug values. Workaround: add a raw `<Thing>Key` field set server-side to the desired slug, and make `Name = ={{<Thing>Key}}`.

data.Title: Using VLOOKUP-style cross-table formulas or reading a related entity's field directly
data.LooksRight: Writing a calculated field that tries to read a field on a related row directly (like a spreadsheet VLOOKUP), instead of going through the declared lookup.
data.ActualFix: There is no native VLOOKUP in calculated formulas; cross-table reads only happen via the FK/lookup pattern (lookup follows the relationship FK) or via SUMIFS/COUNTIFS aggregations in the other direction. Calculated fields on a row only see fields on that same row (including lookups) — reference the lookup field, not the related entity directly.

data.Title: Leaking ERB/DAG/rulebook jargon into the user-facing README
data.LooksRight: Describing the app's mechanics in the README using terms like DAG, calculated field, rulebook, multi-hop, transpiler, inference chain, or calling the edit-build-test cycle 'the loop' / a 'What to add next' section 'the loop's next turns'.
data.ActualFix: README and user-facing docs must read as if you've never heard of Effortless/DAGs/rulebooks — use plain business language ("derived value", "updates automatically", describe the cascade in domain terms). ERB/DAG/transpiler terminology is only allowed in CLAUDE.md and in an optional, clearly-labeled 'How This Was Built' developer-reference section at the very end. The word 'loop' must never appear in the README; the enhancements section must be called 'What to add next' (or a domain variant), not 'next turns of the loop'.

data.Title: Hand-editing generated rulespeak output
data.LooksRight: Directly editing rulespeak/rulespeak.md or rulespeak/rulespeak.html to fix wording, correct a rule description, or tweak formatting — since they're plain readable text files sitting in the repo, it looks like normal doc editing.
data.ActualFix: rulespeak/* is an output spoke regenerated on every `effortless build` from the effortless-rulebook.json hub SSoT. Any hand-edit is silently overwritten on the next build. The fix is to edit the rulebook hub (the formulas/schema) and rebuild, not touch the generated files.

data.Title: Treating RuleSpeak as an optional add-on the user must request
data.LooksRight: Writing/authoring effortless-rulebook.json and declaring the task done without installing rulebook-to-rulespeak or running a build, waiting for the user to separately ask for 'documentation' or 'rulespeak'.
data.ActualFix: RuleSpeak is the default human-readable sibling of every new rulebook, not optional — install rulebook-to-rulespeak and run `effortless build` immediately whenever effortless-rulebook.json is created or first populated, without being asked. Only skip if the user explicitly declines it.

data.Title: Writing local-dev migrations instead of rebuilding from the rulebook
data.LooksRight: Hand-writing an ALTER TABLE / migration script directly against the local-dev SQL Server to make a schema change quickly.
data.ActualFix: NO MIGRATIONS on local-dev SQL Server. Schema changes go through the rulebook → `effortless build` → `init-db.sh`, which regenerates check-add/idempotent T-SQL scripts (not delta migrations) on every build.

data.Title: Reading generated SQL into context to verify a build
data.LooksRight: Catting `sql-server/*.sql` (e.g. `02-create-functions.sql`) into context after a build to check that the generated T-SQL is correct.
data.ActualFix: `effortless build` is atomic — don't read generated `sql-server/*.sql` into context to 'verify'; instead query the live views with `sqlcmd` if you need to check something.

data.Title: Running `-install rulebook-to-sql-server` from the project root
data.LooksRight: Running `effortless -install rulebook-to-sql-server -i ../effortless-rulebook/effortless-rulebook.json` from the project root, since that's where `effortless.json` lives.
data.ActualFix: Must `cd` into `/sql-server/` first. Wrong cwd dumps SQL into the project root and registers the wrong `RelativePath` in `effortless.json`.

data.Title: Assuming the transpiler's default DB name/password in init-db.sh is usable as-is
data.LooksRight: Running `init-db.sh` straight after install, assuming the shipped `DEFAULT_CONN` in `sql-server/init-db.sh` already points at your project's DB name and SA password.
data.ActualFix: The transpiler ships a generic default — patching `DEFAULT_CONN` (dbname + SA password) before first run is explicitly called out as 'this skill's job, not a transpiler bug'.

data.Title: Leaving both Postgres and SQL Server DB-init build steps active when switching substrates
data.LooksRight: Installing rulebook-to-sql-server alongside an existing rulebook-to-postgres/initdb setup without disabling the old Postgres entries, assuming both can coexist in the build.
data.ActualFix: Set `IsDisabled: true` on the `rulebooktopostgres` and `initdb` entries whose `RelativePath` is `/postgres` — only one active DB init should run per build.

data.Title: Treating boolean/decimal semantics as identical between Postgres and SQL Server
data.LooksRight: Filtering with `is_active = true` or summing calc columns directly as if SQL Server booleans/aggregates behave like Postgres.
data.ActualFix: SQL Server booleans in calc columns are often `'1'`/`'0'` nvarchar (normalize in API; filter with `is_active = '1'`), and `SUM()` on calc columns may need `CAST(... AS DECIMAL(38,10))`.

data.Title: Wrong effortless.json key: Transpilers vs ProjectTranspilers
data.LooksRight: Emitting a top-level `Transpilers` array (or `Inputs`/`Outputs`/`InputFile`/`OutputFile`/`Parameters`/`Type`/`Version`/`Source`/`Target`/`TranspilerName`) in effortless.json because those field names sound plausible for a build-config schema.
data.ActualFix: The correct key is `ProjectTranspilers`. None of `Inputs`, `Outputs`, `InputFile`, `OutputFile`, `Parameters`, `Type`, `Version`, `Source`, `Target`, or `TranspilerName` exist in the schema at all — inputs/outputs go via `-i`/`-o` flags in `CommandLine`, parameters via `-p key=value` in `CommandLine`, and the transpiler's identity is just the `Name` field.

data.Title: Hand-writing a transpiler registration instead of using effortless -install
data.LooksRight: Manually authoring a `ProjectTranspilers` entry (with `LastVersionUsed`, `LastUrl`, `Enabled`, etc.) by hand in effortless.json to 'wire up' a transpiler.
data.ActualFix: `effortless -install <transpiler-name> [flags]` is the only correct way to register a transpiler — it must be run from the directory where the transpiler's output should land. `LastVersionUsed` and `LastUrl` are written by the CLI after a run and should not be invented/hand-authored.

data.Title: Leaving rulebook-to-airtable enabled after install
data.LooksRight: Installing `rulebook-to-airtable` (the reverse-sync tool) the same way as any other transpiler and leaving it with default `IsDisabled` state, assuming `effortless build` running it periodically is fine.
data.ActualFix: Every airtable-facing tool MUST include `-account airtable`, and if `rulebook-to-airtable` is wired it MUST have `"IsDisabled": true` set manually if the CLI doesn't do it — it is reverse-sync only and must never run in a normal `effortless build`, only via `effortless build -id`.

data.Title: Reading generated output files to verify a build
data.LooksRight: After running `effortless build`, cat'ing/reading the generated SQL or other output files into context to confirm the build worked, treating it like a normal compile step you should inspect.
data.ActualFix: `effortless build` is fire-and-forget — treat it like `npm install`. Do not read generated files afterward to verify, and do not cat SQL into context.

data.Title: Adding transpiler-specific data by extending effortless.json instead of the rulebook
data.LooksRight: When a transpiler needs more input data than the rulebook currently provides, adding new fields directly to effortless.json (e.g., an ad hoc config blob) to pass that data through.
data.ActualFix: No transpiler may change the IR shape. If a transpiler needs more data, add fields to the rulebook (effortless-rulebook.json), not to effortless.json — the rulebook is the single IR contract every transpiler reads/writes.

data.Title: Reimplementing the Explainer DAG UI instead of using generated output
data.LooksRight: Hand-writing hover cards, toggles, DAG page renderers, an explainer-host.js/explainer-bridge.js bridge module, custom CSS overrides for .dag-cell/.dag-hovercard, a custom Jinja/HTML shell wrapping DAG pages, or patch scripts on generated explainer-dag.js — all things that look like normal frontend work to get the feature polished.
data.ActualFix: The transpiler output IS the UI. Only: install rulebook-to-explainer-dag, run effortless build, serve /rulebook-explainer-dag/* as static files, paste integrate/snippet.html, mark cells with data-er-dag, and call enhanceCells(). Do not create explainer-host.js/explainer-bridge.js (except the sanctioned React §4 pattern), don't override dag.css, don't patch generated explainer-dag.js — fix the transpiler version instead. Host code budget is ~30 lines outside the generated folder.

data.Title: Using the deprecated rulebook-to-react-explainer-dag / <DagCell> transpiler
data.LooksRight: Loading the effortless-react-explainer-dag skill or leaving rulebook-to-react-explainer-dag installed in effortless.json with <DagCell table=... field=...> components, since it sounds like the React-native path.
data.ActualFix: That transpiler and component are deprecated/superseded. Use rulebook-to-explainer-dag + plain data-er-dag markers instead; remove the old transpiler from effortless.json and delete stale web/src/explainer-dag/ if migrating.

data.Title: Assuming Vite HMR refreshes the DAG after a rulebook edit
data.LooksRight: Editing effortless-rulebook.json and expecting the running Vite dev server to hot-reload the updated DAG/RuleSpeak content automatically, since HMR normally picks up file changes.
data.ActualFix: embedded-graph.js is baked at transpile time. You must re-run `./start.sh build` (or `effortless build`) after any rulebook edit — restarting/HMR-ing Vite alone will not refresh it (this is pitfall #1 and also called out after the transpiler table).

data.Title: Wrong casing or snake_case in data-er-dag
data.LooksRight: Writing data-er-dag="invoices.totalDue" or otherwise using the view's snake_case column name / lowercase table name, since that's how the DB/view actually names the field.
data.ActualFix: Must use PascalCase rulebook Table.Field names (matching the rulebook JSON, not the snake_case view column). A casing mismatch fails silently — the ƒ badge just doesn't appear — with no error, so it must be verified against the rulebook JSON directly.

data.Title: Using path routing mode inside a client-routed SPA
data.LooksRight: Using mode: "path" for DAG navigation inside a React/Vue/Svelte SPA because it maps cleanly to /dag/:table/:field-style URLs.
data.ActualFix: path mode has no popstate listener, so a client-side router won't re-render on navigation. SPAs must use mode: "callback" with routing.navigate/navigateTable/fieldHref/tableHref/onBack/onHome wired to the app's own router (§4), driving renderFieldPage/renderTablePage as route components.

data.Title: Wrapping raw editable inputs with data-er-dag
data.LooksRight: Adding data-er-dag markers to every field shown in a form/table for consistency, including raw editable <input> fields.
data.ActualFix: Only calculated/lookup/aggregation values (and the calculated Name PK) should be wrapped — raw fields have no graph, and wrapping them just clutters forms.

data.Title: Deriving HEAD from the promotion_migrations catalog instead of the folders on disk
data.LooksRight: Reading the rulebook's PromotionMigrations catalog table to determine what 'HEAD' is (since it looks like the authoritative list of migrations), and computing the dev/HEAD version from that catalog.
data.ActualFix: HEAD is defined as the newest migration FOLDER on disk (postgres/migrations/<NNNN>-*/). The catalog is only a metadata MIRROR of the folders and can LAG them — a folder can exist and even be applied to staging while its catalog row is missing, freezing a catalog-derived HEAD one release behind. Always enumerate the folders and LEFT-JOIN the catalog for metadata; a folder with no catalog row is a broken build, surfaced loudly, but still counts toward HEAD.

data.Title: Storing 'the version' anywhere instead of deriving it from the ledger on every read
data.LooksRight: Keeping a project_meta field, an erb_versions number, or otherwise treating a cached/stored value (including the catalog table itself) as the authoritative current version, since it's simpler to read than recomputing from migration state each time.
data.ActualFix: The version must be DERIVED from the ledger on every read, never stored as authority: HEAD = newest folder on disk; an env's version = the newest migration in its own schema_migrations. Any stored copy is exactly what drifts and reintroduces the frozen-HEAD bug. erb_versions is a human changelog only (label + message), and a missing row must degrade to the migration id, never freeze or fabricate a version.

data.Title: Writing directly to staging/beta/production from the admin portal ('Save to staging DB')
data.LooksRight: Adding a convenience feature where, when the portal is pointed at staging/beta/production, typing a value into a grid and hitting Save writes directly to that environment's database, just like it does for dev.
data.ActualFix: Staging, beta, and production can ONLY be changed by a ledger-tracked apply.sh migration. When pointed at those tiers the portal is read-and-drive only (inspect, trigger a migration/code push) — there is no other write path. 'If you find one, delete it.'

data.Title: Shipping an auto-generated diff directly as the migration
data.LooksRight: Running a schema/config diff between dev and the target and using the raw diff output (or a machine-generated dump) as the up.sql migration file itself, since the diff already shows exactly what changed.
data.ActualFix: Auto-diffing is fine for DISCOVERY only ('the diff proposes'). A human or agent must hand-derive the up.sql — intentional, idempotent, correctly ordered, self-registering, scoped to schema+config only ('you dispose'). The raw diff must never be the shipped artifact.

data.Title: Creating a migration folder without registering it in the rulebook in the same step
data.LooksRight: Hand-authoring a new postgres/migrations/<NNNN>-<slug>/ folder and treating the rulebook registration (PromotionMigrations row) as a follow-up/cleanup task to do later.
data.ActualFix: The rulebook row must be added in the SAME edit that creates the folder — registering in the rulebook is the ONLY thing that puts the migration in dev's catalog. A folder without a matching row is a bug/broken build. cut-version.sh automates this via register-promotion-migration.mjs; hand-authored folders must add the row immediately.

data.Title: Teaching the Deployment Management page to auto-backfill missing PromotionMigrations rows
data.LooksRight: Having the Deployment page notice a folder with no catalog row and automatically write/reconcile the missing rulebook row for convenience, since it already has the data to do so.
data.ActualFix: The Deployment page NEVER authors the rulebook. It only reads the ledger to grade environments. A folder-without-a-row must be surfaced as a broken build for a human/agent to fix at the source (add the rulebook row + rebuild) — building reconcile logic into the page reintroduces the second-source-of-truth the ledger model exists to kill.

data.Title: Regenerating/rebaselining the 000-seed-rulebook migration to capture new schema state
data.LooksRight: When dev's schema has drifted a lot from the seed, re-dumping current dev over 000-seed-rulebook/up.sql to 'refresh the baseline' and simplify the migration chain.
data.ActualFix: 000-seed is generated ONCE and never regenerated. Every delta from genesis forward becomes a new additive migration (0001, 0002, ...). A regenerated frozen snapshot is exactly the drift anti-pattern this model exists to prevent.

data.Title: Putting rulebook-owned config into a data-injection migration, or operational data into any migration
data.LooksRight: Bundling nav/roles/permissions/config rows into a one-off data-injection migration for convenience, or including live operational data (claims, documents, blobs, assistant turns) in a promotion migration to get a target environment 'fully populated'.
data.ActualFix: Keep the three data classes separate: rulebook config always flows rulebook → generated seed → dev, and reaches staging/beta/prod only via hand-authored config upserts/deletes in a migration; deliberately-omitted large datasets use dedicated data-injection migrations only when meant for that target; operational data never rides the rails — never written back to the rulebook and never included in any migration.

data.Title: Running init-db.sh (or restoring data) against staging/beta/production, or promoting data backward
data.LooksRight: Using the same DROP+reseed init-db.sh script against a staging or remote database to 'quickly sync it up', or restoring staging/production data from a lower environment when troubleshooting.
data.ActualFix: init-db.sh must hard-refuse any non-localhost host and any non-dev DB name — it only ever touches dev. Staging/beta/production move only through apply.sh migrations. Data restores only flow downstream (production → beta/UAT is expected, production → staging is allowed); the reverse direction is never allowed, and a remote is never init-db'd.

data.Title: Hand-editing the generated 00–05*.sql files instead of the rulebook
data.LooksRight: Directly patching a generated SQL file (00-05*.sql) to fix a schema/config issue on dev quickly, since the change is small and the generated file is right there.
data.ActualFix: The rulebook (effortless-rulebook.json) is HEAD/SSoT — edit it and rebuild. If dev ever contradicts the rulebook, that's a pipeline bug to fix in the pipeline, never a hand-patch to dev or its generated files.

data.Title: Grading one tier with a deep drift check and others with only the fast ledger signal
data.LooksRight: Running the expensive full pg_dump/config deep comparison only for the tier currently being investigated (e.g. production) while leaving other tiers on the cheap ledger-position signal, to save time.
data.ActualFix: Grading must be symmetric — the fast signal (ledger + canonical schema fingerprint) applies to every tier the same way, and the deep Drift report, when run, must be run for both/all targets being compared. Never grade one tier deep and another cheap, since asymmetric grading makes the matrix untrustworthy.

data.Title: Using a raw pg_dump hash (not order-independent) to detect drift
data.LooksRight: Comparing raw pg_dump --schema-only output (or its md5) between two environments to decide if they've drifted, since a byte-for-byte diff seems like the strictest check.
data.ActualFix: Must use an order-independent canonical schema hash (normalize the dump: sort objects, strip volatile noise) — a raw pg_dump md5 reports false drift purely from statement ordering, and canonicalization must reflect dev's actual shape (e.g. if dev deliberately lacks certain FKs, HEAD lacks them too) rather than an idealized schema.

data.Title: Hand-rolling cpln apply + manual Deploy click instead of publish-tool.sh
data.LooksRight: Manually running `cpln apply` on the workload and then clicking around in the UI (or otherwise improvising a deploy) because it seems to accomplish the same end result of getting a new version live.
data.ActualFix: There is exactly one supported scripted path: `scripts/publish-tool.sh <transpilerId> <category>/<tool-name>`, which mirrors the green Deploy button exactly (Airtable version record + build/push + cpln apply + wait + activate). Never hand-roll the sequence.

data.Title: Calling the deleted POST /api/transpilers/:id/deploy endpoint
data.LooksRight: Reaching for a direct `curl -X POST /api/transpilers/:id/deploy` because it looks like the natural REST endpoint for triggering a deploy.
data.ActualFix: That endpoint was deleted because it created broken, un-built Airtable records. Use `publish-tool.sh`, which drives the SSE `deploy/stream` endpoint instead.

data.Title: Running build-and-push-cpln-workload.sh and assuming the tool is now published
data.LooksRight: Running `scripts/build-and-push-cpln-workload.sh` and treating it as the publish step since it builds, pushes, and does `cpln apply` — appearing to complete the deploy.
data.ActualFix: That script only builds/pushes the image and applies the workload; it does NOT flip `[latest]` live. The new build is reachable only at its own versioned cpln URL — `effortless build`/`-install` still resolves to the old version until `publish-tool.sh` (or the Deploy button) activates it via `PUT /api/versions/:versionId {IsActive:true}`.

data.Title: Concluding the transpiler-server is down when localhost:3000 doesn't respond
data.LooksRight: Trying `curl localhost:3000` (or the default API_BASE), getting nothing back, and concluding the transpiler-server isn't running / telling the user to start it.
data.ActualFix: The server often runs on a different PORT (e.g. 4205). Find the actual port via `ps aux | grep transpiler-server` then `lsof -nP -p <PID> -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN`, and pass `API_BASE="http://localhost:<port>/api"` to publish-tool.sh before assuming it's down. Also, in the Claude Code sandbox, localhost/*.cpln.app calls can be blocked by the sandbox itself even when the service is up — retry with the sandbox disabled before concluding it's down.

data.Title: Treating a post-publish cold-start GatewayTimeout as a broken tool
data.LooksRight: After publishing, running `effortless -install`/`effortless build` and seeing `Remote transpiler not ready (GatewayTimeout)` → `ERROR: Timed out waiting for cook`, then concluding the freshly published tool is broken/defective.
data.ActualFix: cpln workloads scale to zero, so the first call after publish cold-starts the container — this is a known timing quirk, not a defect. Warm it first with `curl <workloadUrl>/healthz`, optionally confirm via a direct POST + task polling, then re-run install/build.
